In context, probably the best way to look at the potential end of the petrodollar is to see it as one piece of the dollar-based portion of the global economy. Since the 1950s, the dollar has experienced an immense amount of support in terms of global trade and investment and in terms of dollar reserves held by foreigners. This has greatly propped up demand for US debt and for dollars, and this has had enormous disinflationary effects in the domestic US economy. That is, newly created dollars are soaked up by foreigners who both want and need dollars to pay off dollar-denominated debt and to pad bank reserves. But if global dollar dominance truly is in decline, we could potentially expect both higher domestic price inflation and higher interest rates than what Americans have become accustomed to over the past thirty years. In other words, as the dollar declines, the US regime will no longer be able to monetize debt and heap up immense new deficits without fear of high price inflation or falling Treasury prices. The end of the petrodollar is not a reason to panic right now, but it is the latest sign that the US regime’s power via the dollar is being reined in.

## What Is the Petrodollar?

The petrodollar is the result of US efforts to secure access to Middle Eastern oil while also lessening the slide of the dollar in the early 1970s.

By 1974, the US dollar was in a precarious position. In 1971, thanks to profligate spending on both war and domestic welfare programs, the United States could no longer maintain a set global price for gold in line with the Bretton Woods system established in 1944. The value of the dollar in relation to gold fell as the supply of dollars increased as a byproduct of growing deficit spending. Foreign governments and investors began to lose faith in the dollar. 

In response to these developments, Richard Nixon announced that the US would abandon the Bretton Woods system. The dollar began to float against other currencies. Not surprisingly, this devaluation did not restore confidence in the dollar. Moreover, the US had made no effort to rein in deficit spending. So the US needed to continue to find ways to sell government debt without driving up interest rates. That is, the US needed more buyers for its debt. Motivation for a fix grew even more after 1973, when the first oil shock further exacerbated the deficit-fueled price inflation Americans were enduring.

But by 1974, the enormous flood of dollars from the US into Saudi Arabia, the top oil exporter, suggested a solution. Nixon secured an agreement in which the US would buy oil from Saudi Arabia and provide the kingdom military aid and equipment as well. In return, the Saudis would use their dollars to purchase US Treasurys and help finance US budget deficits.

From a public finance point of view, this appeared to be a win-win. The Saudis would receive protection from geopolitical enemies, and the US would get a new place to unload large amounts of government debt. Moreover, the Saudis could park their dollars in relatively safe and reliable investments in the United States. This became known as “petrodollar recycling.” By spending on oil, the US was creating new demand for US debt and US dollars.

As time went on, thanks to Saudi Arabia’s dominance in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), the dollar’s dominance was extended to OPEC overall, which meant that the dollar became the preferred currency for oil purchases worldwide.

This petrodollar arrangement proved to be especially important in the 1970s and 1980s, when Saudi Arabia and the OPEC countries controlled more of the oil trade than they do now. It also closely tied US interests to Saudi interests, ensuring US enmity toward the kingdom’s traditional rivals, such as Iran. 

## The Petrodollar Is a Type of Eurodollar

In terms of its economic role, however, the petrodollar has always just been a type of Eurodollar.

What is a Eurodollar? According to Robert Murphy:

The term Eurodollar actually refers to any US dollar-denominated deposit held at a financial institution outside of the United States, or even a USD deposit held by a foreign bank within the US. It thus has nothing to do with the euro currency, and is not restricted to dollars held in Europe; they are dollar deposits that are not subject to the same regulations as US dollars held by American banks, nor are they guaranteed by FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation) protection (and hence they tend to earn a higher rate of return).

The trade in Eurodollars is huge, although it’s difficult to quantify exactly how huge. One estimate puts Eurodollar assets at around $12 trillion. For context, we can consider that all assets in US banks total about $22 trillion. Or put another way, “offshore dollar banking now amounts to about half of the US total.” So, the Eurodollar economy is very large, and this “dollar zone” is also a key component of many of the world’s leading economies, given that half or more of the world economy lies in that zone.

In contrast, in 2020, the petrodollar trade amounted to less than $3.5 trillion annually. That’s not insignificant, of course, but even a sizable reduction in this amount will not on its own cause global demand for the dollar (relative to other currencies) to collapse. With so many trillions in dollar-denominated loans floating around the global economy, the petrodollar remains only a piece of a larger pie. 

Nevertheless, we could also conclude that the end of the petrodollar is part of a larger and important trend away from the dollar. The relative size of the Eurodollar market

Gulf countries are also afraid of the rise of electric cars replacing the combustible engine driven vehicles in the future.26【44† †www.idsa.in】They are wary of US’ own oil production (including shale oil) and sudden energy independence, and its emergence as a bigger producer of oil and gas than the GCC.27

The Saudi family chose a young leader in Mohammad bin Salman to meet the aspirations of its expanding youth bulge. He has drawn an ambitious economic development plan under its Vision 2030 programme, which was recently hit by the COVID-19 pandemic.28【45† †www.idsa.in】The initiative is critical for the survival of the state because two-thirds of its aspirational and restive population is now under the age of 35.29【46† †www.idsa.in】The US keeps raising issues of human rights, labour laws, religious and gender equality issues that often even affect Saudi mega projects like Neom city and The Line.30【47† †www.idsa.in】However, China is willing to overlook all such issues and seems keen to help Saudi Arabia with its technology, investments and defence cooperation.31【48† †www.idsa.in】Saudi Arabia also thinks it would have more leverage against Iran, if China was on its side.32

There is also a personal grudge between MBS and Biden. As a presidential candidate, Biden had promised to make Saudi Arabia an international “pariah” state over its dismal human rights record and had said he would cut off all arms shipments to Saudi Arabia and had even castigated by saying there is “very little social redeeming value in the present government in Saudi Arabia”.33

Thus, the Saudi rethink on ties with US is quite simple. Even during his visit to Saudi Arabia, President Biden said he had raised the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi during his meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.34

With reduced Western dependence on Saudi oil and the US drawing down its security forces from West Asia, Saudi Arabia feels it is left to fend for itself in its confrontation with Iran, Iraq and Yemeni threats. As the main oil consuming nations of Saudi and GCC oil are now China and India, Saudi Arabia finds little benefit in continuing to trade oil in US dollars and not in its own currency or that of its consumers.35

## The Petrodollar System

This ongoing tension in US–Saudi relations could undermine the petrodollar system and the existing global financial system in its wake.  

Simply put, the petrodollar is the combination of two words “petroleum” and the “US dollar”. Most of the oil traded worldwide today is in US dollars. This arrangement goes back to a 1974 US–Saudi agreement, arrived at in the aftermath of the Yom Kippur War and the subsequent oil embargo imposed by the Gulf states. In June 1974, then US Secretary of State Henry A. Kissinger and then Crown Prince Fahd of Saudi Arabia signed an agreement to establish two joint commissions—the US–Saudi Joint Commission for Economic Cooperation (JCEOR) and the US–Saudi Arabian Joint Security Commission (JSCOR).36

According to these agreements, the US government promised to provide increased economic and military innovation and aid to Saudi Arabia and in exchange Riyadh agreed to exclusively price all of its oil in US dollars.37【49† †www.idsa.in】Thus, any nation that would import Saudi oil was required to exchange their currency to US dollars before completing the transaction. The remaining OPEC countries followed Saudi Arabia’s petrodollar precedent in 1975. 

The US aim in establishing this new petrodollar system was to protect the value of and increase the demand for the US dollar. Countries around the world started purchase of US dollars and kept them as reserves often in US banks to buy oil for their country, which made the greenback strong and the reserve currency of the world. Other commodities, such as gold, copper, agricultural products, natural gas, etc., are today also traded in US dollars. The rising strength of the US dollar had many world leaders and economists worried for a long time. It was former French finance minister Valéry Giscard d’Estaing who first alleged that the US enjoyed an “exorbitant privilege” on account of the reserve status of its currency.38

The US dollar, though, fell precipitously in value after President Richard Nixon decoupled the currency from the gold peg in 1971. It found a new support in the proverbial ‘black gold’ or petroleum. This started the age of the petrodollar.39

It is the peg of the US dollar to petroleum, which has started shaking again with major oil producers like Saudi Arabia, Russia (now a major producer of petroleum) and other OPEC Plus countries increasingly trading oil in currencies other than the US dollar. Even India and Russia plan to drop all use of the US dollar and the euro in bilateral settlements and conduct all trade transactions in rupee and rouble, a senior Russian official has said.40

It is worth noting that Saudi Arabia, whose oil customers are now mainly China and India, has recently evinced interest in joining BRICS, a grouping which includes Saudi Arabia’s major oil markets—India and China. The issue of expansion of the bloc will be on the agenda of the BRICS Summit scheduled to take place in South Africa this year.41

# Saudi Arabia to End Petrodollar Pact

### Gesara.news » 【1†News】 » Saudi Arabia to End Petrodollar Pact

Share via: 【3† †www.facebook.com】  【4† †www.twitter.com】  【5† †api.whatsapp.com】

[Image 1] 

In June 2024, Saudi Arabia is expected to announce that it will cease all oil sales in US dollars, marking the end of the 50-year Petrodollar Pact signed on June 6, 1974, which expires on June 9, 2024.  
The decision not to renew this pact stems from Saudi Arabia's recent invitation to BRICS and its move towards dedollarization.  
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has informed the Saudi government that the country will no longer accept US dollars for oil transactions.  
This shift includes considerations to accept other currencies, such as the Chinese yuan, for oil sales, as reported by the Wall Street Journal on March 15, 2022.

BRICS nations are considering a stablecoin for international trade settlements.  
Sergei Ryabkov, Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister, hails this move as groundbreaking.  
He also states that BRICS is also exploring a platform for digital payments.  
Ryabkov: "BRICS is moving forward, creating an important precedent."  
Russia has also hinted at issuing a 【7†gold-backed stablecoin】.  
With member nations amassing gold reserves, the idea gains traction.

Fed policies that are coming soon on inflation, and interest rate suppression will be rocket fuel for gold and silver. And gold and silver are just getting started. If Bitcoin is $10,000 per unit, why cannot gold be $5,000, $10,000 or $15,000 per ounce? With the amount of dollars out there, it could easily be $5,000 or $8,000 per ounce, and that is where it is headed. The bond market will eventually collapse, but the biggest collapse coming is the faith in all fiat currencies.

Biblical Nephilim giants walking with POTUS?  
Is it the same guy in Dan Scavino cover pic (in front of airplane)?  
We have good extraterrestrials beings protecting POTUS!  
Sources:【11†twitter.com/1wokeindividual†twitter.com】, 【12†facebook.com/reven.rising.7†facebook.com】

Donald Trump: With your help, we carried out the largest tax and regulation cuts, by far, in American history. And they now want to quadruple tax us, and they want to quadruple, and beyond, the regulation cuts. And when we say "tax" and we say "regulation" and you say, Oh, tax cuts. That's so wonderful, - but the people in this room that are the heads of industry - you have some very powerful people in this room - they know that the regulation cuts may have been even more important than the biggest tax cuts we've ever had.   
Source:【14†twitter.com/WhiteHouse†twitter.com】

#### 【15†Ramaswamy supports Trump and commodity-backed currency】

Billionaire entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy claims BRICS is developing a gold-backed currency to replace the U.S. dollar as the world's primary reserve currency.

This would permanently increase our borrowing cost if the dollar is no longer the established reserve currency of the world.  
So yes, actually, that does matter. The right way to deal with it, though, is not to try to swat that down, but increase the value proposition of the dollar itself by pegging the dollar to hard commodities," he stated in a press conference.  
Vivek Ramaswamy dropped out of the presidential race and endorsed Donald Trump. Known for supporting currencies backed by commodities, his alliance with Trump suggests a shared vision for economic stability and challenges to traditional fiat systems.

In context, probably the best way to look at the potential end of the petrodollar is to see it as one piece of the dollar-based portion of the global economy. Since the 1950s, the dollar has experienced an immense amount of support in terms of global trade and investment and in terms of dollar reserves held by foreigners. This has greatly propped up demand for US debt and for dollars, and this has had enormous disinflationary effects in the domestic US economy. That is, newly created dollars are soaked up by foreigners who both want and need dollars to pay off dollar-denominated debt and to pad bank reserves. But if global dollar dominance truly is in decline, we could potentially expect both higher domestic price inflation and higher interest rates than what Americans have become accustomed to over the past thirty years. In other words, as the dollar declines, the US regime will no longer be able to monetize debt and heap up immense new deficits without fear of high price inflation or falling Treasury prices. The end of the petrodollar is not a reason to panic right now, but it is the latest sign that the US regime’s power via the dollar is being reined in.

## What Is the Petrodollar?

The petrodollar is the result of US efforts to secure access to Middle Eastern oil while also lessening the slide of the dollar in the early 1970s.

By 1974, the US dollar was in a precarious position. In 1971, thanks to profligate spending on both war and domestic welfare programs, the United States could no longer maintain a set global price for gold in line with the Bretton Woods system established in 1944. The value of the dollar in relation to gold fell as the supply of dollars increased as a byproduct of growing deficit spending. Foreign governments and investors began to lose faith in the dollar. 

In response to these developments, Richard Nixon announced that the US would abandon the Bretton Woods system. The dollar began to float against other currencies. Not surprisingly, this devaluation did not restore confidence in the dollar. Moreover, the US had made no effort to rein in deficit spending. So the US needed to continue to find ways to sell government debt without driving up interest rates. That is, the US needed more buyers for its debt. Motivation for a fix grew even more after 1973, when the first oil shock further exacerbated the deficit-fueled price inflation Americans were enduring.

But by 1974, the enormous flood of dollars from the US into Saudi Arabia, the top oil exporter, suggested a solution. Nixon secured an agreement in which the US would buy oil from Saudi Arabia and provide the kingdom military aid and equipment as well. In return, the Saudis would use their dollars to purchase US Treasurys and help finance US budget deficits.

From a public finance point of view, this appeared to be a win-win. The Saudis would receive protection from geopolitical enemies, and the US would get a new place to unload large amounts of government debt. Moreover, the Saudis could park their dollars in relatively safe and reliable investments in the United States. This became known as “petrodollar recycling.” By spending on oil, the US was creating new demand for US debt and US dollars.

As time went on, thanks to Saudi Arabia’s dominance in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), the dollar’s dominance was extended to OPEC overall, which meant that the dollar became the preferred currency for oil purchases worldwide.

This petrodollar arrangement proved to be especially important in the 1970s and 1980s, when Saudi Arabia and the OPEC countries controlled more of the oil trade than they do now. It also closely tied US interests to Saudi interests, ensuring US enmity toward the kingdom’s traditional rivals, such as Iran. 

## The Petrodollar Is a Type of Eurodollar

In terms of its economic role, however, the petrodollar has always just been a type of Eurodollar.

What is a Eurodollar? According to Robert Murphy:

The term Eurodollar actually refers to any US dollar-denominated deposit held at a financial institution outside of the United States, or even a USD deposit held by a foreign bank within the US. It thus has nothing to do with the euro currency, and is not restricted to dollars held in Europe; they are dollar deposits that are not subject to the same regulations as US dollars held by American banks, nor are they guaranteed by FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation) protection (and hence they tend to earn a higher rate of return).

The trade in Eurodollars is huge, although it’s difficult to quantify exactly how huge. One estimate puts Eurodollar assets at around $12 trillion. For context, we can consider that all assets in US banks total about $22 trillion. Or put another way, “offshore dollar banking now amounts to about half of the US total.” So, the Eurodollar economy is very large, and this “dollar zone” is also a key component of many of the world’s leading economies, given that half or more of the world economy lies in that zone.

In contrast, in 2020, the petrodollar trade amounted to less than $3.5 trillion annually. That’s not insignificant, of course, but even a sizable reduction in this amount will not on its own cause global demand for the dollar (relative to other currencies) to collapse. With so many trillions in dollar-denominated loans floating around the global economy, the petrodollar remains only a piece of a larger pie.

The Saudi family chose a young leader in Mohammad bin Salman to meet the aspirations of its expanding youth bulge. He has drawn an ambitious economic development plan under its Vision 2030 programme, which was recently hit by the COVID-19 pandemic.28【45† †www.idsa.in】The initiative is critical for the survival of the state because two-thirds of its aspirational and restive population is now under the age of 35.29【46† †www.idsa.in】The US keeps raising issues of human rights, labour laws, religious and gender equality issues that often even affect Saudi mega projects like Neom city and The Line.30【47† †www.idsa.in】However, China is willing to overlook all such issues and seems keen to help Saudi Arabia with its technology, investments and defence cooperation.31【48† †www.idsa.in】Saudi Arabia also thinks it would have more leverage against Iran, if China was on its side.32

There is also a personal grudge between MBS and Biden. As a presidential candidate, Biden had promised to make Saudi Arabia an international “pariah” state over its dismal human rights record and had said he would cut off all arms shipments to Saudi Arabia and had even castigated by saying there is “very little social redeeming value in the present government in Saudi Arabia”.33

Thus, the Saudi rethink on ties with US is quite simple. Even during his visit to Saudi Arabia, President Biden said he had raised the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi during his meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.34

With reduced Western dependence on Saudi oil and the US drawing down its security forces from West Asia, Saudi Arabia feels it is left to fend for itself in its confrontation with Iran, Iraq and Yemeni threats. As the main oil consuming nations of Saudi and GCC oil are now China and India, Saudi Arabia finds little benefit in continuing to trade oil in US dollars and not in its own currency or that of its consumers.35

## The Petrodollar System

This ongoing tension in US–Saudi relations could undermine the petrodollar system and the existing global financial system in its wake.  

Simply put, the petrodollar is the combination of two words “petroleum” and the “US dollar”. Most of the oil traded worldwide today is in US dollars. This arrangement goes back to a 1974 US–Saudi agreement, arrived at in the aftermath of the Yom Kippur War and the subsequent oil embargo imposed by the Gulf states. In June 1974, then US Secretary of State Henry A. Kissinger and then Crown Prince Fahd of Saudi Arabia signed an agreement to establish two joint commissions—the US–Saudi Joint Commission for Economic Cooperation (JCEOR) and the US–Saudi Arabian Joint Security Commission (JSCOR).36

According to these agreements, the US government promised to provide increased economic and military innovation and aid to Saudi Arabia and in exchange Riyadh agreed to exclusively price all of its oil in US dollars.37【49† †www.idsa.in】Thus, any nation that would import Saudi oil was required to exchange their currency to US dollars before completing the transaction. The remaining OPEC countries followed Saudi Arabia’s petrodollar precedent in 1975. 

The US aim in establishing this new petrodollar system was to protect the value of and increase the demand for the US dollar. Countries around the world started purchase of US dollars and kept them as reserves often in US banks to buy oil for their country, which made the greenback strong and the reserve currency of the world. Other commodities, such as gold, copper, agricultural products, natural gas, etc., are today also traded in US dollars. The rising strength of the US dollar had many world leaders and economists worried for a long time. It was former French finance minister Valéry Giscard d’Estaing who first alleged that the US enjoyed an “exorbitant privilege” on account of the reserve status of its currency.38

The US dollar, though, fell precipitously in value after President Richard Nixon decoupled the currency from the gold peg in 1971. It found a new support in the proverbial ‘black gold’ or petroleum. This started the age of the petrodollar.39

It is the peg of the US dollar to petroleum, which has started shaking again with major oil producers like Saudi Arabia, Russia (now a major producer of petroleum) and other OPEC Plus countries increasingly trading oil in currencies other than the US dollar. Even India and Russia plan to drop all use of the US dollar and the euro in bilateral settlements and conduct all trade transactions in rupee and rouble, a senior Russian official has said.40

### Likelihood of Saudi Arabia Maintaining Non-Renewal Position on Petrodollar Pact

1. **Alignment with BRICS and Dedollarization Trends**: Saudi Arabia's interest in joining BRICS and the broader dedollarization trend indicates a strategic move away from US dollar dependency. The kingdom's participation in BRICS initiatives, such as developing a new reserve currency, supports the likelihood that it will maintain its non-renewal stance on the petrodollar pact【9†source】【11†source】.

2. **Economic Diversification and Vision 2030**: Under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia is focused on diversifying its economy away from oil dependency. Embracing alternative currencies for oil transactions aligns with this vision, enhancing economic resilience and reducing reliance on the US dollar【9†source】【11†source】.

3. **Geopolitical Tensions with the US**: Ongoing geopolitical tensions between the US and Saudi Arabia, including issues related to human rights and regional security dynamics, make it less likely that Saudi Arabia will revert to the petrodollar system. These tensions encourage Saudi Arabia to seek stronger economic and political ties with other major powers like China and Russia【9†source】【11†source】.

4. **Growing Influence of China and India**: As China and India become the primary consumers of Saudi oil, it is strategically beneficial for Saudi Arabia to trade in their currencies. This shift reduces transaction costs and builds stronger economic partnerships, making the continuation of the non-renewal stance more probable【9†source】【11†source】.

5. **Global Financial System Evolution**: The evolution of the global financial system towards multipolarity, with increasing use of digital currencies and alternative payment systems, aligns with Saudi Arabia's move away from the petrodollar. This broader trend makes the non-renewal of the petrodollar pact consistent with the kingdom's long-term economic strategy【10†source】【11†source】.

Given these factors, it is highly likely that Saudi Arabia will maintain its position on not renewing the petrodollar pact, favoring a diversified and resilient economic strategy.

The Saudi family chose a young leader in Mohammad bin Salman to meet the aspirations of its expanding youth bulge. He has drawn an ambitious economic development plan under its Vision 2030 programme, which was recently hit by the COVID-19 pandemic.28【45† †www.idsa.in】The initiative is critical for the survival of the state because two-thirds of its aspirational and restive population is now under the age of 35.29【46† †www.idsa.in】The US keeps raising issues of human rights, labour laws, religious and gender equality issues that often even affect Saudi mega projects like Neom city and The Line.30【47† †www.idsa.in】However, China is willing to overlook all such issues and seems keen to help Saudi Arabia with its technology, investments and defence cooperation.31【48† †www.idsa.in】Saudi Arabia also thinks it would have more leverage against Iran, if China was on its side.32

There is also a personal grudge between MBS and Biden. As a presidential candidate, Biden had promised to make Saudi Arabia an international “pariah” state over its dismal human rights record and had said he would cut off all arms shipments to Saudi Arabia and had even castigated by saying there is “very little social redeeming value in the present government in Saudi Arabia”.33

Thus, the Saudi rethink on ties with US is quite simple. Even during his visit to Saudi Arabia, President Biden said he had raised the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi during his meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.34

With reduced Western dependence on Saudi oil and the US drawing down its security forces from West Asia, Saudi Arabia feels it is left to fend for itself in its confrontation with Iran, Iraq and Yemeni threats. As the main oil consuming nations of Saudi and GCC oil are now China and India, Saudi Arabia finds little benefit in continuing to trade oil in US dollars and not in its own currency or that of its consumers.35

## The Petrodollar System

This ongoing tension in US–Saudi relations could undermine the petrodollar system and the existing global financial system in its wake.  

Simply put, the petrodollar is the combination of two words “petroleum” and the “US dollar”. Most of the oil traded worldwide today is in US dollars. This arrangement goes back to a 1974 US–Saudi agreement, arrived at in the aftermath of the Yom Kippur War and the subsequent oil embargo imposed by the Gulf states. In June 1974, then US Secretary of State Henry A. Kissinger and then Crown Prince Fahd of Saudi Arabia signed an agreement to establish two joint commissions—the US–Saudi Joint Commission for Economic Cooperation (JCEOR) and the US–Saudi Arabian Joint Security Commission (JSCOR).36

According to these agreements, the US government promised to provide increased economic and military innovation and aid to Saudi Arabia and in exchange Riyadh agreed to exclusively price all of its oil in US dollars.37【49† †www.idsa.in】Thus, any nation that would import Saudi oil was required to exchange their currency to US dollars before completing the transaction. The remaining OPEC countries followed Saudi Arabia’s petrodollar precedent in 1975. 

The US aim in establishing this new petrodollar system was to protect the value of and increase the demand for the US dollar. Countries around the world started purchase of US dollars and kept them as reserves often in US banks to buy oil for their country, which made the greenback strong and the reserve currency of the world. Other commodities, such as gold, copper, agricultural products, natural gas, etc., are today also traded in US dollars. The rising strength of the US dollar had many world leaders and economists worried for a long time. It was former French finance minister Valéry Giscard d’Estaing who first alleged that the US enjoyed an “exorbitant privilege” on account of the reserve status of its currency.38

The US dollar, though, fell precipitously in value after President Richard Nixon decoupled the currency from the gold peg in 1971. It found a new support in the proverbial ‘black gold’ or petroleum. This started the age of the petrodollar.39

It is the peg of the US dollar to petroleum, which has started shaking again with major oil producers like Saudi Arabia, Russia (now a major producer of petroleum) and other OPEC Plus countries increasingly trading oil in currencies other than the US dollar. Even India and Russia plan to drop all use of the US dollar and the euro in bilateral settlements and conduct all trade transactions in rupee and rouble, a senior Russian official has said.40

## BRICS and the New Reserve Currency

It is worth noting that Saudi Arabia, whose oil customers are now mainly China and India, has recently evinced interest in joining BRICS, a grouping which includes Saudi Arabia’s major oil markets—India and China. The issue of expansion of the bloc will be on the agenda of the BRICS Summit scheduled to take place in South Africa this year.41

[Image 1] 

In June 2024, Saudi Arabia is expected to announce that it will cease all oil sales in US dollars, marking the end of the 50-year Petrodollar Pact signed on June 6, 1974, which expires on June 9, 2024.  
The decision not to renew this pact stems from Saudi Arabia's recent invitation to BRICS and its move towards dedollarization.  
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has informed the Saudi government that the country will no longer accept US dollars for oil transactions.  
This shift includes considerations to accept other currencies, such as the Chinese yuan, for oil sales, as reported by the Wall Street Journal on March 15, 2022.

BRICS nations are considering a stablecoin for international trade settlements.  
Sergei Ryabkov, Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister, hails this move as groundbreaking.  
He also states that BRICS is also exploring a platform for digital payments.  
Ryabkov: "BRICS is moving forward, creating an important precedent."  
Russia has also hinted at issuing a 【7†gold-backed stablecoin】.  
With member nations amassing gold reserves, the idea gains traction.

#### 【8†Fed policies will be rocket fuel for gold and silver】

Fed policies that are coming soon on inflation, and interest rate suppression will be rocket fuel for gold and silver. And gold and silver are just getting started. If Bitcoin is $10,000 per unit, why cannot gold be $5,000, $10,000 or $15,000 per ounce? With the amount of dollars out there, it could easily be $5,000 or $8,000 per ounce, and that is where it is headed. The bond market will eventually collapse, but the biggest collapse coming is the faith in all fiat currencies.   
Sources:【9†usawatchdog.com†usawatchdog.com】

#### 【10†Biblical Nephilim giants around Trump?】

Biblical Nephilim giants walking with POTUS?  
Is it the same guy in Dan Scavino cover pic (in front of airplane)?  
We have good extraterrestrials beings protecting POTUS!  
Sources:【11†twitter.com/1wokeindividual†twitter.com】, 【12†facebook.com/reven.rising.7†facebook.com】

#### 【13†The largest tax and regulation cuts in history】

Donald Trump: With your help, we carried out the largest tax and regulation cuts, by far, in American history. And they now want to quadruple tax us, and they want to quadruple, and beyond, the regulation cuts. And when we say "tax" and we say "regulation" and you say, Oh, tax cuts. That's so wonderful, - but the people in this room that are the heads of industry - you have some very powerful people in this room - they know that the regulation cuts may have been even more important than the biggest tax cuts we've ever had.   
Source:【14†twitter.com/WhiteHouse†twitter.com】

Billionaire entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy claims BRICS is developing a gold-backed currency to replace the U.S. dollar as the world's primary reserve currency.

Vivek Ramaswamy dropped out of the presidential race and endorsed Donald Trump. Known for supporting currencies backed by commodities, his alliance with Trump suggests a shared vision for economic stability and challenges to traditional fiat systems.

It is the peg of the US dollar to petroleum, which has started shaking again with major oil producers like Saudi Arabia, Russia (now a major producer of petroleum) and other OPEC Plus countries increasingly trading oil in currencies other than the US dollar. A biogas or biomethane production facility typically consists of several key components designed to facilitate the anaerobic digestion process, biogas upgrading, and distribution of the produced biomethane. Here are the main components:

1. **Feedstock Reception and Pre-processing:** This is where the organic material, such as agricultural waste, food waste, or sewage sludge, is received and prepared for digestion. Pre-processing may involve shredding, chopping, or mixing the feedstock to optimize its suitability for digestion and ensure a consistent feedstock composition.

2. **Anaerobic Digesters:** These are the heart of the biogas production process. Anaerobic digesters are large, sealed tanks or vessels where microorganisms break down the organic material in the absence of oxygen, producing biogas as a byproduct. There are different types of anaerobic digesters, including continuous stirred-tank reactors (CSTRs), plug-flow digesters, and covered lagoons, each with its own advantages and applications.

3. **Biogas Storage:** Biogas produced in the anaerobic digesters is typically stored in gas storage tanks or domes before further processing. This allows for the collection and temporary storage of biogas until it can be utilized or upgraded.

4. **Biogas Upgrading System:** Biogas upgrading is the process of purifying the raw biogas to remove impurities such as carbon dioxide (CO2), hydrogen sulfide (H2S), moisture, and other contaminants, resulting in high-purity biomethane. Common biogas upgrading technologies include water scrubbing, pressure swing adsorption (PSA), amine scrubbing, and membrane separation.

5. **Biomethane Compression and Storage:** Once the biogas is upgraded to biomethane, it may undergo compression to increase its pressure for storage and transportation. Biomethane can be compressed and stored in high-pressure tanks or cylinders, or it can be liquefied (liquefied biomethane or LBM) for easier storage and transport.

6. **Gas Grid Injection or On-site Utilization:** Biomethane can be injected directly into the natural gas grid for distribution to end-users, such as residential, commercial, or industrial consumers. Alternatively, it can be used on-site for power generation, heating, or as a transportation fuel for vehicles equipped with natural gas engines.

7. **Digestate Handling and Management:** After the anaerobic digestion process, the leftover organic material, known as digestate, is typically separated from the liquid effluent and may undergo further treatment or processing. Digestate can be used as a nutrient-rich fertilizer for agriculture or composting, helping to close the nutrient loop and improve soil health.

These components work together to create a closed-loop system where organic waste is converted into renewable energy (biomethane) and nutrient-rich byproducts, contributing to sustainable waste management and reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

Yes, waste from a hog farm can indeed be a suitable and abundant source of raw material for producing biomethane through anaerobic digestion. Here's why:

1. **High Organic Content:** Hog farm waste, including manure and other organic residues, is rich in organic matter, which makes it an excellent feedstock for anaerobic digestion. This organic material serves as a substrate for the microorganisms involved in the anaerobic digestion process, facilitating the production of biogas.

2. **Abundance:** Hog farms produce large quantities of waste on a continuous basis. Anaerobic digestion provides a means to efficiently manage and utilize this waste stream, reducing environmental impacts associated with waste disposal while simultaneously producing renewable energy.

3. **Nutrient Management:** Anaerobic digestion not only converts hog farm waste into renewable energy but also helps manage nutrients within the waste. The digestion process can reduce the concentration of pathogens in the manure, making it safer for land application as fertilizer. Additionally, the resulting digestate can serve as a nutrient-rich soil amendment, closing the nutrient loop and improving soil health.

4. **Environmental Benefits:** By capturing methane emissions from hog farm waste through anaerobic digestion, the production of biomethane helps mitigate greenhouse gas emissions. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, and its capture and conversion into biomethane for energy use can significantly reduce the carbon footprint of hog farming operations.

5. **Energy Independence:** Utilizing hog farm waste to produce biomethane provides an opportunity for energy independence and diversification. Instead of relying solely on traditional fossil fuels, hog farmers can generate their own renewable energy onsite, reducing dependence on external energy sources and potentially lowering operational costs in the long run.

Overall, hog farm waste represents a valuable resource for biomethane production, offering environmental, economic, and operational benefits for both the farming industry and the broader renewable energy sector.

A biomethane production facility is a complex industrial site designed to convert organic waste into renewable energy in the form of methane gas, also known as biomethane or renewable natural gas (RNG). Here's a description of such a facility:

1. **Feedstock Reception and Pre-processing Area:**
   - The facility typically begins with a reception area where various organic materials are delivered. These materials may include agricultural waste, food waste, sewage sludge, or energy crops.
   - Upon arrival, the feedstock undergoes pre-processing, which may involve shredding, grinding, or chopping to optimize its suitability for digestion and ensure uniformity in the feedstock composition.

2. **Anaerobic Digestion System:**
   - The pre-processed feedstock is then directed to anaerobic digesters, which are large, sealed tanks or vessels where the anaerobic digestion process occurs.
   - Within the digesters, microorganisms break down the organic material in the absence of oxygen, producing biogas as a byproduct. This biogas consists primarily of methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2), along with traces of other gases.

3. **Biogas Storage:**
   - The biogas produced in the anaerobic digesters is collected and temporarily stored in gas storage tanks or domes located onsite.
   - These storage facilities allow for the accumulation of biogas until it can be further processed or utilized.

4. **Biogas Upgrading and Purification:**
   - The raw biogas undergoes upgrading and purification to remove impurities and increase the concentration of methane, producing high-purity biomethane.
   - Common biogas upgrading technologies include water scrubbing, pressure swing adsorption (PSA), amine scrubbing, or membrane separation.

5. **Biomethane Compression and Storage:**
   - Once upgraded, the biomethane may undergo compression to increase its pressure for storage and transportation.
   - Biomethane can be stored in high-pressure tanks or cylinders onsite, or it can be liquefied (liquefied biomethane or LBM) for easier storage and transport.

6. **Distribution or Utilization:**
   - The biomethane produced at the facility can be injected directly into the natural gas grid for distribution to end-users.
   - Alternatively, it can be utilized onsite for power generation, heating, or as a transportation fuel for vehicles equipped with natural gas engines.

7. **Digestate Handling and Management:**
   - After the anaerobic digestion process, the leftover organic material, known as digestate, is separated from the liquid effluent.
   - The digestate may undergo further treatment or processing before being used as a nutrient-rich fertilizer for agriculture or composting.

Throughout the facility, rigorous monitoring and control systems are in place to optimize the anaerobic digestion process, ensure safety, and maximize the efficiency of biomethane production. These facilities play a crucial role in sustainable waste management and the transition towards renewable energy sources.

Yes, used cooking oil (UCO) can be used as a feedstock for making bio-methanol. Here is a brief overview of the process and its advantages:

### Overview

1. **Collection and Preparation**: Used cooking oil is collected from various sources, such as restaurants and food processing industries. It is then filtered and cleaned to remove impurities and solid residues.

2. **Conversion Process**:
    - **Transesterification**: The cleaned UCO undergoes a transesterification process where it is reacted with methanol in the presence of a catalyst (usually sodium or potassium hydroxide). This reaction produces biodiesel and glycerol.
    - **Glycerol to Bio-methanol**: The glycerol, a byproduct of the biodiesel production process, can be further processed through gasification or reforming to produce bio-methanol. In gasification, the glycerol is subjected to high temperatures in the presence of steam to produce synthesis gas (syngas), a mixture of hydrogen and carbon monoxide. This syngas is then catalytically converted to methanol.

3. **Bio-methanol Production**: The syngas derived from glycerol is converted to bio-methanol using a catalyst, typically copper-based. This process occurs at high pressures and temperatures.

### Advantages

1. **Sustainability**: Using UCO as feedstock for bio-methanol production supports waste recycling and reduces the environmental impact associated with the disposal of used cooking oil.

2. **Reduced Carbon Footprint**: Bio-methanol production from UCO emits fewer greenhouse gases compared to conventional fossil fuel-derived methanol, contributing to lower overall carbon emissions.

3. **Economic Benefits**: Utilizing waste cooking oil as a feedstock can be cost-effective and provides an additional revenue stream for businesses that generate large quantities of used cooking oil.

4. **Energy Efficiency**: The conversion process is energy-efficient, and the produced bio-methanol can be used as a renewable fuel or chemical feedstock in various industrial applications.

When considering the efficiency and energy value of converting used cooking oil (UCO) into biodiesel versus methanol, several factors need to be taken into account. Here's a comparison of both options:

### Energy Content

1. **Biodiesel**:
   - **Energy Content**: Biodiesel has an energy content of about 37.8 MJ/kg (megajoules per kilogram).
   - **Production Process**: UCO undergoes a relatively straightforward transesterification process to produce biodiesel. The process is well-established and efficient.

2. **Methanol**:
   - **Energy Content**: Methanol has an energy content of about 19.9 MJ/kg.
   - **Production Process**: Producing methanol from UCO involves several steps: transesterification to produce biodiesel and glycerol, gasification of glycerol to produce syngas, and finally, methanol synthesis from syngas. This process is more complex and energy-intensive.

### Efficiency and Practical Considerations

1. **Production Complexity**:
   - **Biodiesel**: The production of biodiesel from UCO is simpler and requires fewer steps, resulting in lower energy consumption and higher overall efficiency.
   - **Methanol**: The conversion process to methanol involves multiple steps with higher energy requirements and potential energy losses at each stage.

2. **Energy Value per Unit**:
   - **Biodiesel**: Given its higher energy content per kilogram, biodiesel provides more energy per unit of mass compared to methanol.
   - **Methanol**: Although methanol has a lower energy content per kilogram, it can be used in certain applications where its lower boiling point and higher volatility are advantageous.

3. **End-Use Applications**:
   - **Biodiesel**: Can be used directly as a fuel in diesel engines with little to no modification. It is a drop-in replacement for conventional diesel fuel.
   - **Methanol**: Requires modifications for use in internal combustion engines or can be used as a feedstock for producing other chemicals and fuels.

### Environmental Considerations

1. **Biodiesel**: Produces fewer greenhouse gases and pollutants compared to conventional diesel. It is biodegradable and less toxic.
2. **Methanol**: Can be produced sustainably but may involve more complex handling and storage requirements due to its toxicity and corrosive nature.

### Conclusion

Based on energy content and production efficiency, **biodiesel** is generally the more efficient option for converting UCO. It has a higher energy value per unit and a simpler production process compared to methanol. Biodiesel also offers the advantage of being a direct replacement for conventional diesel fuel, making it easier to integrate into existing fuel infrastructure.

The technology used for converting used cooking oil (UCO) to bio-methanol can also be applied to wood, but it involves different processes and requires significant equipment changes and modifications. Here's a detailed comparison:

### Technology for UCO to Bio-Methanol

1. **Collection and Preparation**: UCO is filtered and cleaned.
2. **Transesterification**: UCO undergoes transesterification to produce biodiesel and glycerol.
3. **Glycerol Gasification**: Glycerol is gasified to produce syngas.
4. **Methanol Synthesis**: Syngas is converted to methanol using a catalyst.

### Technology for Wood to Bio-Methanol

1. **Collection and Preparation**: Wood is collected, chipped, and dried.
2. **Gasification**: Wood is gasified directly to produce syngas. This involves thermal decomposition at high temperatures in the presence of a controlled amount of oxygen or steam.
3. **Syngas Cleaning**: The produced syngas needs to be cleaned to remove impurities such as tar, particulates, and sulfur compounds.
4. **Methanol Synthesis**: Clean syngas is converted to methanol using a catalyst.

### Required Equipment Changes and Modifications

1. **Feedstock Handling and Preparation**:
    - **For Wood**: Requires equipment for chipping, drying, and possibly grinding the wood. This includes wood chippers, dryers, and grinders.
    - **For UCO**: Involves filtration and cleaning systems for the oil.

2. **Gasification**:
    - **For Wood**: A biomass gasifier designed to handle solid feedstock like wood. This gasifier must operate at high temperatures and may include a fluidized bed or entrained flow design.
    - **For UCO**: If using glycerol from biodiesel production, a separate gasification system designed for liquid feedstocks is required.

3. **Syngas Cleaning**:
    - **For Wood**: More extensive cleaning systems are needed to handle the impurities in syngas produced from wood. This may include scrubbers, filters, and catalytic tar reformers.
    - **For UCO**: The syngas from glycerol is generally cleaner but still requires some level of purification.

4. **Methanol Synthesis**:
    - **For Both**: The methanol synthesis reactor and associated catalysts are similar for both feedstocks. However, the syngas composition and purity requirements might necessitate adjustments in the process conditions and catalyst choice.

### Summary

While the basic principle of converting syngas to methanol remains the same, the front-end processes for converting UCO and wood to syngas are significantly different. Converting a plant designed for UCO to handle wood would require substantial changes in feedstock preparation, gasification, and syngas cleaning equipment.

An executive compensation package typically consists of various components designed to attract, motivate, and retain top-level executives. While the specific components may vary depending on the company and industry, here are some typical elements found in executive compensation packages:

1. Base Salary: This is the fixed amount of money that an executive receives for their services. It forms the foundation of their compensation package.

2. Annual Bonus: Executives may be eligible for an annual performance-based bonus tied to predetermined goals, such as financial targets or individual performance metrics. The bonus amount often represents a percentage of the executive's base salary.

3. Long-Term Incentives: These are typically provided in the form of equity-based compensation to align the interests of executives with those of shareholders. Long-term incentives include stock options, restricted stock units (RSUs), performance shares, or stock appreciation rights (SARs). These awards usually vest over time or are tied to specific performance targets.

4. Equity Grants: Executives may receive periodic grants of company shares or options as part of their compensation package. These grants may be subject to a vesting schedule or other conditions.

5. Performance-Based Cash Awards: In addition to long-term incentives, executives may be eligible for cash awards based on the company's performance relative to predetermined targets. These awards often serve as an additional performance-based incentive.

6. Retirement Plans: Companies may offer retirement benefits, such as 401(k) plans or defined benefit pension plans, to provide long-term financial security for executives.

7. Perquisites (Perks): Executives often receive various additional benefits, commonly referred to as perks. These can include things like company cars, housing allowances, club memberships, personal use of corporate aircraft, financial planning services, or executive health and wellness programs.

8. Severance and Change-in-Control Arrangements: Executives may have severance packages in place that outline the terms and conditions of their departure from the company, including financial compensation and benefits. Change-in-control arrangements may provide additional compensation or protections in the event of a merger, acquisition, or other significant corporate transaction.

9. Insurance and Health Benefits: Executives may receive comprehensive health insurance coverage, life insurance, disability insurance, and other related benefits as part of their compensation package.

It's important to note that executive compensation practices can vary significantly across different companies and industries. The structure and components of executive compensation packages are subject to regulations, governance guidelines, and the principles of transparency and shareholder interests.

N.C. releases general biogas permit despite environmental justice concerns

by Cameron Oglesby, Southerly
July 12, 2022

This story is the second in a series about biogas development in eastern North Carolina. Read the first here.

Almost every aspect of the hog farming industry has a footprint in Sampson County, N.C. Growers contracted with Smithfield Foods are required to use feed processed and stored in Turkey. The floor slats used in hog houses—open grates that hog feces, urine, and other fluids flow through—are produced by several facilities across the county. And in the heart of Clinton is the Smithfield Foods processing plant, where hogs are trucked in, killed, and processed. 

On a sunny day in late April, Sherri White-Williamson, director of the Environmental Justice Community Action Network (EJCAN), drove Duke University students around Sampson County to see these impacts: Sign after sign lining the roads marking entrances to family farms; swaths of trees hiding massive concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) and waste lagoons; open fields where machines spray brown liquid—fertilizer made from hog waste—on crops. 

White-Williamson has focused lately on educating the public about biogas, an energy production method that caps open waste lagoons and captures methane to turn into natural gas. The swine industry—and increasingly state and federal politicians—says biogas is a boon to communities and the environment because it reduces the amount of methane seeping into the atmosphere from hog waste lagoons.

However, community organizers, residents, and researchers are concerned the North Carolina legislature’s well-documented, long-standing relationship with the swine industry is allowing lenient policies that will further harm communities already suffering health and environmental impacts from industrial hog farming. 

On July 1, the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality (NCDEQ)—the state’s environmental regulator—issued general biogas permits for swine, cattle, and wet poultry operations, allowing them to bypass individual water quality review and public hearing processes when installing an anaerobic digester on their lagoons. The permits are in effect until Sept. 2024.

“We’re disappointed that the general permit is not more protective of the communities that EJCAN works with, but we will continue to advocate on behalf of the citizens who remain concerned about the possibility of contamination and exposure to high levels of pollutants,” White-Williamson said.

The permits reduce communities’ ability to weigh in on individual projects and will fast-track biogas operations in the state. Environmental groups

With tens of billions of gallons of manure produced by hogs per year, waste is a massive problem. Biogas is becoming an increasingly popular way to address it: 【47†Last November†www.whitehouse.gov】, President Joe Biden’s administration pointed to biogas operations as a key way to reduce methane emissions in agriculture. 

Powerful institutions in North Carolina, including Duke University and Duke Energy, have been exploring the viability of biogas production since 2010, three years after the state mandated 12.5% of energy must come from renewable sources starting in 2021. This same law stated that by 2025, 0.2% of this renewable energy must come from swine waste-to-energy sources. That’s enough to power a little less than 122,000 North Carolina homes each year. 

Smithfield’s major project, 【48†Align Renewable Natural Gas (RNG)†alignrng.com】, would install anaerobic digesters on farms in Virginia, Utah, and North Carolina, connecting them via pipeline systems to processing plants for “cleaning” and conversion of waste gasses into usable methane. From there, the gas is moved through existing natural gas infrastructure.

The North Carolina section, called the Grady Road project, would comprise more than 30 miles of pipelines—the exact location of which Smithfield has not shared—that 【44†c†grist.org】onnect 19 hog farms in Duplin and Sampson Counties to a natural gas processing plant at the intersection of Highway 24 and I-40, between Warsaw and Turkey. 

Smithfield says the Align project is expected to capture about 85,000 tons of methane each year and will produce enough energy to power 700,000 homes over 20 years. 

“The Align RNG initiative provides new income potential to North Carolina family farmers by turning one of their biggest costs—hog manure—into a new revenue source,” Kraig Westerbeek, senior director of Smithfield Renewables and hog production environmental affairs, wrote in an email. “In addition to directly benefiting local farmers, these projects benefit the surrounding community by creating jobs, bolstering local tax bases, and driving greater economic development.”

However, the Grady Road Project would only create 2.5 permanent jobs, and any jobs associated with building the digesters or pipelines are temporary, 【49†according to NC Policy Watch†ncpolicywatch.com】. Smithfield has stated local farmers will be compensated through long-term contracts. Align RNG declined to be interviewed but agreed to answer questions via email. Rather than responding specifically to nine questions, Kraig Westerbeek, vice president of Smithfield Renewables, said in a statement:  

“Modern hog farming is a result of continuous research and innovation, which allows farmers to provide the best care for their animals, protect the environment and ensure food safety for consumers. The benefits of covered lagoons and digestors are well-documented and clear. They are capturing otherwise fugitive emissions and converting them to renewable energy, which is only positive for the environment and the local community. Our project in Sampson and Duplin Counties will reduce annual greenhouse gas emissions from participating farms by more than 150,000 metric tons each year. That’s the same as taking 36,000 cars off the road each year. Even skeptics of this project cannot deny this is a major environmental improvement.”

Westerbeek noted that numerous federal agencies, including the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, have long encouraged the use of biodigesters, and that more than 20 other hog farm operations in North Carolina “have installed the same technology without any of the harmful impacts opponents have predicted.” The biogas project, he said, will also bring new income to North Carolina farmers by providing an additional revenue source.

But Ryke Longest, clinical professor of law and director of the Environmental Law and Policy Clinic at Duke University School of Law, said the key issue is not the use of the biodigesters but the far more important matter of Smithfield’s failure to properly treat the billions of tons of hog waste. He compared the process that Align and Smithfield are using to fitting a car with a tailpipe when a catalytic converter — in this case, modern waste treatment — is widely available.  

> Those living near hog farms complain of choking odors. One woman said her laundry drying on the line is often flecked with manure. 

“They’re basically just putting a tailpipe on and not cleaning up the fundamental source of the pollution — the waste itself,” says Longest. “All that’s being removed from the farm is the gas, leaving behind these other two waste streams that need to be addressed. These systems were designed, in some cases, 30 or 40 years ago and were allowed to continue to operate under a grandfathering provision under some assumptions that have never really been tested.”

For those, like Roberta McCalop, who live in close proximity to the hog farms, the burden of the operations is ever present. In addition to the choking odors, minute fecal particles from the lagoons and field spraying operations pollute the air; one resident who declined to use her name complained that her laundry drying on the line is often flecked with manure. Nitrogen from the unlined pits seeps into waterways and contributes to groundwater and well pollution, increasing the frequency and intensity of algal blooms and fish kills.

Residents also experience documented health effects. A 【14†study†www.ncmedicaljournal.com】 conducted by the Environmental Health Scholars program at Duke University School of Medicine found that communities located near hog CAFOs had higher overall and infant mortality, as well as mortality due to anemia, kidney disease, tuberculosis, and septicemia. The communities also had higher hospital admissions, ER visits, and low-birthweight infants.

Still, Smithfield has never followed through on its agreement to get rid of the lagoon and spray field system. A decade ago, the North Carolina General Assembly acknowledged the harm this method caused and said that Smithfield must employ new waste management technology to address those problems. Digestate from the reactors is routed back to the farms and stored in the existing wastewater lagoons prior to land application. Odors from the land application of raw swine manure have been contentious in eastern NC and the digestate from the reactors likely has a much lower odor profile due to the anaerobic degradation of volatile fatty acids in AD, although no odor-specific evaluations have been conducted.  
Each farm is outfitted with a low-power compressor that pulls the biogas from beneath the covers, filters it to remove particulates, and removes the moisture through a condenser. The preconditioned biogas is routed to a central gas clean-up facility on Smithfield Foods’ property (about 3 miles distance from the farms) through low-pressure piping. Each farm is equipped with emergency flares if there is an operational issue with the central facility.

#### Gas Clean-Up

The gas clean-up system (nicknamed “GUS”) consists of pressure-swing absorption to remove carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide and other constituents. The cleaned biomethane is pressurized to 100 lbs/square inch (psi) to be sold to Duke Energy via a subsidiary, Piedmont Natural Gas, which operates the natural gas distribution network in eastern NC. The pipeline injection standards are typically rigorous (see “【28†Pipeline Injection of Biomethane in California】” March/April 2018) and real-time gas analyzers on both sides of the interconnection monitor gas quality. Table 1 compares Optima’s gas quality to the injection specifications.  
Optima KV entered into a 15-year agreement with Duke Energy to produce 80,000 MMBTUs/year of RNG. This will create about 11,000 megawatt-hours (MWh) of power produced at Duke Energy’s natural gas-fired plants in in Wayne and New Hanover Counties. The biomethane produced by the Optima KV project will partially replace the fossil-fuel natural gas consumed by those two electricity generation stations (an approach known as “directed biogas”).

#### North Carolina REPS

North Carolina’s Renewable Energy Portfolio Standard (REPS) became law in 2007. It requires investor-owned utilities (like Duke Energy) to generate up to 12.5 percent of their energy needs through renewable energy resources and energy efficiency programs by 2020. The law also requires utilities to use hog wastes to generate a portion of their renewable energy requirements, however, this has been delayed several times due to the lack of a hog waste-to-energy infrastructure. In 2017, utilities were required to generate 0.07 percent (around 91,000 MWh) of their renewable energy from hog wastes, and that percentage rises to 0.2 percent (more than 200,000 MWh) by 2019.  
In March 2012, the North Carolina Utilities Commission approved the use of directed biogas to generate renewable energy certificates for compliance with the REPS on the basis of the biogas’ electricity-generating potential. The electricity generating potential of the biomethane is based on the assumption that it will be used to fuel a natural gas-powered facility, thereby greatly increasing the electricity generation potential of the biomethane as compared with on-site power generation.  
In an effort to accelerate deployment of swine waste-to-energy projects, Duke University commissioned a spatial-economic optimization study to evaluate options for meeting the REPS requirement. The study developed an iterative geospatial and economic analysis to optimize the configuration of swine waste-to-energy production on the basis of the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) of specific production scenarios, including on-farm and centralized options. Four options were evaluated:  
• On-farm electricity production  
• On-farm biomethane collection and pipeline injection (“individual farm-directed biomethane”)  
• Centralized electricity production at a hub supplied with biogas from a high-density cluster of swine operations (“centralized electricity production”)  
• Injection of biomethane into the natural gas grid from a central gas upgrade unit fed by biogas from multiple farms (“centralized directed biogas”)  
Using the LCOEs derived for each scenario, the researchers ranked them on the basis of cost-effectiveness, testing mixed digesters against covered lagoons as well as high versus low cost estimates for inter-farm biogas transport and pipeline injection. Of the four scenarios, the most cost-effective were centralized directed biogas and on-farm electricity production; estimated costs for the former were sometimes nearly half those of on-farm production, where in-ground ambient temperature mixed anaerobic digesters were assumed to be in use. Overall, the costs of the directed biogas scenario, which was the most cost-effective scenario in many cases, ranged between $0.111/kilowatt hour (kWh) and $0.058/kWh (2013 dollars).

Pipeline injection of biomethane can be advantageous over direct on-farm generation of electricity for sale to the grid. While injection depends on the availability of a nearby pipeline infrastructure with adequate capacity and the gas upgrading equipment can be expensive, direct sales of electricity to the grid are hampered by low purchase prices, the reality that electrical distribution systems are designed as radial networks delivering power in a unidirectional way from substations to consumers,

N.C. releases general biogas permit despite environmental justice concerns

by Cameron Oglesby, Southerly
July 12, 2022

This story is the second in a series about biogas development in eastern North Carolina. Read the first here.

Almost every aspect of the hog farming industry has a footprint in Sampson County, N.C. Growers contracted with Smithfield Foods are required to use feed processed and stored in Turkey. The floor slats used in hog houses—open grates that hog feces, urine, and other fluids flow through—are produced by several facilities across the county. And in the heart of Clinton is the Smithfield Foods processing plant, where hogs are trucked in, killed, and processed. 

On a sunny day in late April, Sherri White-Williamson, director of the Environmental Justice Community Action Network (EJCAN), drove Duke University students around Sampson County to see these impacts: Sign after sign lining the roads marking entrances to family farms; swaths of trees hiding massive concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) and waste lagoons; open fields where machines spray brown liquid—fertilizer made from hog waste—on crops. 

White-Williamson has focused lately on educating the public about biogas, an energy production method that caps open waste lagoons and captures methane to turn into natural gas. The swine industry—and increasingly state and federal politicians—says biogas is a boon to communities and the environment because it reduces the amount of methane seeping into the atmosphere from hog waste lagoons.

However, community organizers, residents, and researchers are concerned the North Carolina legislature’s well-documented, long-standing relationship with the swine industry is allowing lenient policies that will further harm communities already suffering health and environmental impacts from industrial hog farming. 

On July 1, the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality (NCDEQ)—the state’s environmental regulator—issued general biogas permits for swine, cattle, and wet poultry operations, allowing them to bypass individual water quality review and public hearing processes when installing an anaerobic digester on their lagoons. The permits are in effect until Sept. 2024.

“We’re disappointed that the general permit is not more protective of the communities that EJCAN works with, but we will continue to advocate on behalf of the citizens who remain concerned about the possibility of contamination and exposure to high levels of pollutants,” White-Williamson said.

Digestate from the reactors is routed back to the farms and stored in the existing wastewater lagoons prior to land application. Odors from the land application of raw swine manure have been contentious in eastern NC and the digestate from the reactors likely has a much lower odor profile due to the anaerobic degradation of volatile fatty acids in AD, although no odor-specific evaluations have been conducted.  
Each farm is outfitted with a low-power compressor that pulls the biogas from beneath the covers, filters it to remove particulates, and removes the moisture through a condenser. The preconditioned biogas is routed to a central gas clean-up facility on Smithfield Foods’ property (about 3 miles distance from the farms) through low-pressure piping. Each farm is equipped with emergency flares if there is an operational issue with the central facility.

#### Gas Clean-Up

The gas clean-up system (nicknamed “GUS”) consists of pressure-swing absorption to remove carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide and other constituents. The cleaned biomethane is pressurized to 100 lbs/square inch (psi) to be sold to Duke Energy via a subsidiary, Piedmont Natural Gas, which operates the natural gas distribution network in eastern NC. The pipeline injection standards are typically rigorous (see “【28†Pipeline Injection of Biomethane in California】” March/April 2018) and real-time gas analyzers on both sides of the interconnection monitor gas quality. Table 1 compares Optima’s gas quality to the injection specifications.  
Optima KV entered into a 15-year agreement with Duke Energy to produce 80,000 MMBTUs/year of RNG. This will create about 11,000 megawatt-hours (MWh) of power produced at Duke Energy’s natural gas-fired plants in in Wayne and New Hanover Counties. The biomethane produced by the Optima KV project will partially replace the fossil-fuel natural gas consumed by those two electricity generation stations (an approach known as “directed biogas”).

#### North Carolina REPS

North Carolina’s Renewable Energy Portfolio Standard (REPS) became law in 2007. It requires investor-owned utilities (like Duke Energy) to generate up to 12.5 percent of their energy needs through renewable energy resources and energy efficiency programs by 2020. The law also requires utilities to use hog wastes to generate a portion of their renewable energy requirements, however, this has been delayed several times due to the lack of a hog waste-to-energy infrastructure. In 2017, utilities were required to generate 0.07 percent (around 91,000 MWh) of their renewable energy from hog wastes, and that percentage rises to 0.2 percent (more than 200,000 MWh) by 2019.  
In March 2012, the North Carolina Utilities Commission approved the use of directed biogas to generate renewable energy certificates for compliance with the REPS on the basis of the biogas’ electricity-generating potential. The electricity generating potential of the biomethane is based on the assumption that it will be used to fuel a natural gas-powered facility, thereby greatly increasing the electricity generation potential of the biomethane as compared with on-site power generation.  
In an effort to accelerate deployment of swine waste-to-energy projects, Duke University commissioned a spatial-economic optimization study to evaluate options for meeting the REPS requirement. The study developed an iterative geospatial and economic analysis to optimize the configuration of swine waste-to-energy production on the basis of the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) of specific production scenarios, including on-farm and centralized options. Four options were evaluated:  
• On-farm electricity production  
• On-farm biomethane collection and pipeline injection (“individual farm-directed biomethane”)  
• Centralized electricity production at a hub supplied with biogas from a high-density cluster of swine operations (“centralized electricity production”)  
• Injection of biomethane into the natural gas grid from a central gas upgrade unit fed by biogas from multiple farms (“centralized directed biogas”)  
Using the LCOEs derived for each scenario, the researchers ranked them on the basis of cost-effectiveness, testing mixed digesters against covered lagoons as well as high versus low cost estimates for inter-farm biogas transport and pipeline injection. Of the four scenarios, the most cost-effective were centralized directed biogas and on-farm electricity production; estimated costs for the former were sometimes nearly half those of on-farm production, where in-ground ambient temperature mixed anaerobic digesters were assumed to be in use. Overall, the costs of the directed biogas scenario, which was the most cost-effective scenario in many cases, ranged between $0.111/kilowatt hour (kWh) and $0.058/kWh (2013 dollars).

Pipeline injection of biomethane can be advantageous over direct on-farm generation of electricity for sale to the grid. For a detailed case study on a hypothetical large-scale biomethane plant in Eastern North Carolina, the following references would be useful:

1. **Arthur D. Little's Viewpoint on Biomethane**: Offers insights on biomethane production investments, including ROIs, opportunities, and challenges, especially in the context of advanced biofuels and the role of digestate as a by-product of anaerobic digestion in biomethane production【6†source】.

2. **The State of Biogas and Biomethane Production**: This provides a comprehensive overview of directives and strategies, like the European Methane Strategy, which could be relevant in understanding regulatory frameworks and emissions reduction targets that might affect a biomethane plant【7†source】.

3. **A Review of Biomethane Production**: Discusses the integration of renewable energies in biomethane production and explores various modeling approaches, which can be critical in designing and optimizing a biomethane plant【8†source】.

4. **IEA's Outlook for Biogas and Biomethane to 2040**: This report discusses the broader implications of biogas and biomethane in the context of global energy demands, the limitations of electrification, and the role of gas infrastructure in a low-emissions system【9†source】.

5. **Biogas and Biomethane – Renewables 2023**: Offers insights into the benefits of biomethane, its use in decarbonizing sectors, and its role in circular economy and rural development【10†source】.

These references provide a holistic view of the biomethane industry, covering technological, economic, environmental, and regulatory aspects. They should serve as a solid foundation for a detailed case study on a large-scale biomethane plant.

Most GoO trades are still mainly conducted “over the counter” (not listed or traded on a major stock exchange), resulting in low price transparency and high volatility. Despite these factors, some clear trends are beginning to emerge. In the most developed markets, such as Denmark or the Netherlands, the GoO for waste-based biomethane is almost twice as valuable as a GoO for food-crop biomethane. With natural gas prices around €50 per MWh, the GoOs are now more valuable than the commodity they represent.

The GoO market used to be mostly voluntary, with sustainability conscious companies buying GoOs to sell “green” gas products or make their gas consumption greener, thus improving their environmental, social, and governance (ESG) scores. But RED II put in place a mandate for fuel suppliers to ensure advanced biofuels (including biomethane) comprise at least 3.5% of road and rail fuel consumption by 2030. This requirement is pushing oil companies to access these markets, thus creating demand for GoOs. The national requirement to create standardized GoO platforms to make consumers aware of the renewable content of their renewable gases will foster those national markets. Since all platforms will be linked though the European Renewal Gas Registry (ERGaR) platform, the individual national markets will become interconnected and GoO will help to create a fostering biomethane development at the European level.

Who should be interested in investing in biomethane production? The answer is quite simple: anyone who wishes to benefit from ROIs of 10% or more. However, certain industries may find easier success in this venture. For example, those in the oil and gas, transportation, and energy utilities sectors may leverage their existing operational models, customer networks, and infrastructure to create synergy and improve their financial performance. Additionally, private equities and infrastructure funds can use their professional management and investments in automation to optimize plant operations and further improve financial performance. Therefore, these industries should consider making biomethane production a top priority in their investment plans.
