## Abstract

:

Anaerobic Digestion (AD) is a well-established process that is becoming increasingly popular, especially as a technology for organic waste treatment; the process produces biogas, which can be upgraded to biomethane, which can be used in the transport sector or injected into the natural gas grid. Considering the sensitivity of Anaerobic Digestion to several process parameters, mathematical modeling and numerical simulations can be useful to improve both design and control of the process. Therefore, several different modeling approaches were presented in the literature, aiming at providing suitable tools for the design and simulation of these systems. The purpose of this study is to analyze the recent advancements in the biomethane production from different points of view. Special attention is paid to the integration of this technology with additional renewable energy sources, such as solar, geothermal and wind, aimed at achieving a fully renewable biomethane production. In this case, auxiliary heat may be provided by solar thermal or geothermal energy, while wind or photovoltaic plants can provide auxiliary electricity. Recent advancements in plants design, biomethane production and mathematical modeling are shown in the paper, and the main challenges that these fields must face with are discussed. Considering the increasing interest of industries, public policy makers and researchers in this field, the efficiency and profitability such hybrid renewable solutions for biomethane production are expected to significantly improve in the next future, provided that suitable subsidies and funding policies are implemented to support their development.

However, there are limits to how quickly and extensively electrification can occur, as electricity is not well suited to deliver all types of energy services. Even if the complete technical potential for electrification were deployed, there would still be sectors requiring other energy sources (given today’s technologies).

For example, most of the world’s shipping, aviation, heavy-freight trucks and certain industrial processes are not yet “electric-ready”. While in the future these sectors could use fuels that have been generated using electricity (such as hydrogen or synthetic fuels), some of these fuels would need a separate delivery infrastructure.

The energy security value of overlapping infrastructure can also be an important consideration for policy makers. Maintaining a parallel gas infrastructure system adds a layer of resilience compared with an approach that relies exclusively on electricity. This was visible, for example, in Japan when gas-fired generation stepped in to provide power following the shutdown of its nuclear reactors from 2011. It also provides a useful hedge against the risks that electrification and the development of new electricity networks do not increase at the pace needed to displace existing fuels while meeting energy service demands.

However, if gas infrastructure is to secure its role in a low-emissions system, it will ultimately need to deliver truly low-carbon energy sources.

#### Electricity cannot be the only vector for the energy sector’s transformation …

### Final energy consumption by carrier in the Sustainable Development Scenario, 2018 and 2040

#### … but can gas infrastructure be repurposed to deliver low-carbon energy?

In the SDS, the share of electricity in final consumption rises from 19% today to 30% by 2040, and there is a simultaneous decarbonisation of supply through a significant expansion of renewables, particularly wind and solar PV but also bioenergy, hydropower and nuclear. Still, half of final energy consumption in 2040 remains served by liquids and gases; the share of low-carbon sources in liquids supply also rises to 14%, and in gas supply to 18%.

Replicating the services that gas grids provide via low-carbon electricity may be possible in some parts of the world, in particular areas that have ample resources to generate renewable electricity, relatively limited winter heating requirements, and an economic base (services and certain industrial subsectors) that is amenable to electrification. However, elsewhere, substituting electricity for gas as a way to provide services to end consumers is likely to be much more challenging and expensive.

There are practical issues with deploying electric heating at scale in both industry and residential sectors. Apart from being a clean domestic energy source, biogases (biogas and biomethane) provide other benefits. For instance, biomethane can be used to decarbonise hard-to-electrify sectors such as transport and industry. Both biogas and biomethane use reduces not only CO_{2} emissions from fossil fuel combustion but also, when correctly managed, methane emissions from the waste and agriculture/livestock sectors (responsible for 60% of anthropogenic global methane emissions). This advantage aligns well with the emissions reduction objectives of the Global Methane Pledge launched in 2021 and signed by 155 countries (as of January 2024). 

Thus, using biogas and biomethane helps build a circular economy around residue and waste valorisation, contributes to rural economic development and creates employment. Plus, producing natural fertilisers as a co­product of biogas and biomethane production can augment farmers’ income and help re‑­­­­establish soil health by eliminating certain environmental impacts related to untreated manure use. Biogas can also be used for clean cooking in developing countries.  

### Main uses of biogases for selected countries and regions, 2021

【112† Open expand 】 

#### Biogas forecast

In the People's Republic of China (hereafter "China"), household digesters were developed some decades ago to provide clean energy for cooking and residential use in rural areas (accounting for around 300 000 TJ/year of biogas production). Impressively, thanks to investment support from the Chinese Rural Household Biogas State Debt Project beginning in 2003, almost 42 million household digesters had been installed by 2015. In 2015, however, government policy shifted towards engineered plants for combined heat and power generation, with capital aid and feed-in tariffs being offered. 

More recently, since 2019 the Chinese government has been steering a biogas industry transition, investing in large-scale (>10 mcm/year) bio-natural gas (BNG, biomethane) projects. These plants would use rural and urban waste feedstocks in an integrated manner to produce electricity and gas to inject into the grid. 

China actively developed new policies in 2022 with its 14th Five-Year Plan for Renewable Energy Development. Impressively, thanks to investment support from the Chinese Rural Household Biogas State Debt Project beginning in 2003, almost 42 million household digesters had been installed by 2015. In 2015, however, government policy shifted towards engineered plants for combined heat and power generation, with capital aid and feed-in tariffs being offered. 

More recently, since 2019 the Chinese government has been steering a biogas industry transition, investing in large-scale (>10 mcm/year) bio-natural gas (BNG, biomethane) projects. These plants would use rural and urban waste feedstocks in an integrated manner to produce electricity and gas to inject into the grid. 

China actively developed new policies in 2022 with its 14th Five-Year Plan for Renewable Energy Development. Although the biogas targets of previous five-year plans for renewable energy were not achieved, revitalisation of the sector is expected for three reasons: national and international energy companies (PetroChina, China Three Gorges Corporation, China General Nuclear Power Group, French company Air Liquide and German company EnviTec Biogas AG) 【113†are beginning to invest in biogas†www.cedigaz.org】; policy support has been strengthened; and grid access has been improved. When designing a 30,000-barrel barge for carrying methanol, there are several design types that can be considered, each with its own advantages and specific applications. Here are three different design types:

1. **Single-Hull Design**: 
   - **Description**: This is the traditional design where the barge consists of a single outer hull. The cargo is stored directly in tanks within this hull.
   - **Pros**: Generally less expensive and simpler to construct. Offers more cargo capacity due to less space taken up by double hulls.
   - **Cons**: Less safe compared to double-hull designs, especially for carrying hazardous materials like methanol. More vulnerable to spills and environmental damage in case of hull breach.

2. **Double-Hull Design**:
   - **Description**: This design features a second hull layer around the main cargo tanks, creating a space between the two hulls. It's a standard design for tankers and barges carrying hazardous materials.
   - **Pros**: Provides additional protection against spills and leaks, enhancing environmental safety. Required by many regulations for hazardous cargo transport.
   - **Cons**: More expensive to build and maintain. The double hull reduces cargo capacity as it takes up more space.

3. **Barge-within-a-Barge Design**:
   - **Description**: This is a variation of the double-hull design where an inner barge is encased within a larger outer barge hull. The space between the two barges can be substantial, providing additional safety.
   - **Pros**: Offers high levels of safety and environmental protection. In case of a breach in the outer hull, the inner barge remains intact.
   - **Cons**: The most expensive of the three designs. It also has a lower cargo capacity due to the substantial space between the inner and outer barges.

Each design type has to be chosen based on the trade-offs between cost, safety, environmental impact, and compliance with regulations.

3. **Onions**: Onions add a nice sharpness to salsa. You could plant about 10 to 12 onion sets or bulbs. You might want to consider both red and white onions for variety.

# Timber is big business in Alabama

From seeding to selling, a look at the state's forest products industry

By

【45†Emmett Burnett】

- 

January 7, 2022

[Image 0] A mix of pine and hardwood thrives on a timber farm in Alabama’s Black Belt.

I think that I shall never see, a poem as lovely as a tree. Poet Joyce Kilmer was correct. Trees are stunning, and in Alabama, lucrative.

According to the 【46†Alabama Forestry Commission†forestry.alabama.gov】’s Forest Inventory Analysis Data, the state’s 23 million acres of forested land is larger than Connecticut, Delaware, Massachusetts, New Jersey and Rhode Island combined. Approximately 93% of it is privately owned.

In 2019, Alabama exported $1.3 billion in forest products. From farmer to factory, many hands nurture and move these products.

This is their story, Alabama’s wood industry, men and women going out on a limb — sometimes literally.

In the world of wood, misconceptions abound. “Many people compare our trees to the rainforest or old growth,” says Ashley Smith, director of education programs for the 【47†Alabama Forestry Association†www.alaforestry.org】. “It is not true. Our climate and growth patterns are different here.” She adds that much of Alabama’s timberland has been here for years, cut for agriculture long before most of us were born.

- Sponsor -

“Our soil is fabulous for tree growth,” says Smith. Therefore, tree farms flourish. Red Hill Farm is one such fertile entity, owned by husband-and-wife team, Trice and Johnnie Nichols.

The couple has farmed their 900 acres near Prattville for about two decades, growing pine and hardwood on land that has been in Johnnie’s family since the 1850s. 

“Pines grow from seedling to 70 feet tall in 30 years,” Trice says. “A tree is similar to livestock,” he continues. “In the earlier stages of life, you ‘fatten it up,’ with plenty of water and rich soil to make the tree bigger, faster.”

Pines are rotated, thinned and sold throughout the life cycle, but as a rule, the taller the better. At its maximum height, pines reach telephone pole category — the most valuable and very marketable. Loggers take it from there.

“I love being in the woods,” says forester Earl Edmondson, of 【48†Harrison Forestry†harrisonforestry.com】/Harrison and Sons Logging in Maplesville. “The business is more mechanized now.”

His schedule is straightforward. “When the weather is dry, we haul wood.” His crews average about 156,000 tons of logs annually, spanning 22 Alabama counties.

Co-owners of Montgomery’s 【49†Legacy Land and Timber LLC†www.linkedin.com】, Bobby Loughridge and Donald Clark agree about logging’s mechanization. “Insurance companies don’t want to see us in the woods ripping trees,” Loughridge notes. “We are much less hands-on.”

In the tree business, the logger is the broker, with contracts between farmers and sawmills and factories. Once delivered, logs become raw materials and the magic happens. Alabama trees become products for the world — timber, plywood, wood pulp, paper, liner board, sawdust, poles, crossties, lumber and more.

Wood becomes commodity at the state’s major players, including 【50†Georgia-Pacific†www.gp.com】, 【51†International Paper†www.internationalpaper.com】, 【52†Packaging Corp. of America†www.packagingcorp.com】, 【53†WestRock†www.westrock.com】, 【54†Kronospan†www.kronospan-worldwide.com】, Brown-Forman Cooperage, Louisiana-Pacific, 【55†Weyerhaeuser†www.weyerhaeuser.com】, 【56†Westervelt†www.westervelt.com】 and 【57†Great Southern Wood Preserving†www.yellawood.com】.

[Image 1] Trice Nichols of Red Hill Farm.

Newer entries to the market are 【58†Rex Lumber†www.rexlumber.com】, Abbeville Fiber, 【59†Jasper Lumber†jasperlumber.com】 and Westervelt’s new Thomasville mill.

Nothing is wasted. From bark to sawdust, every component of a tree is marketable. Though each factory marches to the beat of a different saw, Alabama mills are challenged with evolving markets, increased operating costs and the erratic supply and demand issues from COVID.

“We have seen increased demand from the DIY markets in 2020 and 2021,” said Georgia-Pacific spokesperson Erica-  
Denise Solomon. “That market has pushed volume up across the board in all of our building products businesses.” GP has six facilities across Alabama.

As some markets increased, others — once staples of the industry — are dramatically shrinking. Paper, once the cornerstone of sawmills, is one such commodity. Data once written is now stored electronically. Georgia-Pacific exited the communication paper business in 2019.

Meanwhile in Abbeville, life is good for YellaWood. “We run all the time,” says Michael Lancaster, vice president of sawmill operations at Abbeville Fiber. The facility opened in summer 2019 and joins other mills supplying 15 Great Southern Wood treating plants.

“We were having a good year even before COVID,” recalls Great Southern Wood’s Ryan Blalock, chief purchasing officer. “But once the coronavirus hit, markets plunged and so did lumber supplies. But people were homebound and wanted to make improvements.”

He continues, “Suddenly, demand for YellaWood soared. We had weeks trying to supply the outrageous demand for wood.”

Today Great Southern’s supply and demand are gradually lining out but issues remain with fuel costs and staffing. “Fuel effects our loggers, truckers, suppliers, almost all phases of the business,” says Blalock. “We are seeing those costs rise dramatically.”

“Labor is also a problem,” he notes. “Fortunately, we have a group who is our backbone, but for additional growth it’s now difficult finding additional workers.”

With a January 2021 startup, one of Alabama’s newest mills is Westervelt in Thomasville, the sister plant of Westervelt in Moundville. “Production has been a struggle,” says Mark Richardson, sales and marketing director in the company’s wood products division. “We hired a full crew, but because of COVID, we were unable to conduct planned training in our Moundville plant for new Thomasville employees.”

Westervelt’s Woodlands Director Dave Donaldson adds, “I still think from a supply chain standpoint we are 18 to 24 months away (from normality). The swing may be less but we still have to deal with interruptions due to a next variant.”

Westervelt’s markets include the construction industry through building component manufacturers like truss makers, building material distribution yards and pressure treaters. 

From the newest to one of the oldest, 【60†Scotch Plywood Co†www.scotchplywood.com】.’s origins trace back to Clarke County, 1888. Today, two Alabama sites, Fulton Plywood Mill and Beatrice Mill, have a combined workforce of more than 400 employees.

“Our peak production is generally May through October,” says company Vice President Gray Skipper. “[Sales] demand goes in cycles. February through May.” He adds, “September and October are also big for us as people are rushing to make home additions, repairs and projects before winter snow hits in our Northeast and Midwest markets.”

New technologies and new uses for wood are emerging in Alabama, too, as companies create substitutes for coal. The list includes Zilkha Biomass Energy, Alabama Pellets (【61†Pinnacle Renewable Energy†www.pinnaclepellet.com】) and, coming soon to Sumter County, 【62†Enviva†www.envivabiomass.com】.

With a projected 2023 startup date, Enviva is designed to produce more than one million metric tons per year of wood pellets. The site will be the largest wood pellet production plant in the world.

“Alabama has been supportive for business and industry,” says Rick Frederick, Enviva’s Gulf Coast community relations manager. “The state provides a combination of skilled workforce, raw natural resources and tremendous terminal and port access to the Gulf, such as the 【63†Port of Mobile†www.asdd.com】. It’s a match made in heaven.”

Finally, the finished product, wood in all forms, goes to market by trucking domestically, or from tree to shining sea.

# Timber is big business in Alabama

From seeding to selling, a look at the state's forest products industry

By

【45†Emmett Burnett】

- 

January 7, 2022

[Image 0] A mix of pine and hardwood thrives on a timber farm in Alabama’s Black Belt.

I think that I shall never see, a poem as lovely as a tree. Poet Joyce Kilmer was correct. Trees are stunning, and in Alabama, lucrative.

According to the 【46†Alabama Forestry Commission†forestry.alabama.gov】’s Forest Inventory Analysis Data, the state’s 23 million acres of forested land is larger than Connecticut, Delaware, Massachusetts, New Jersey and Rhode Island combined. Approximately 93% of it is privately owned.

In 2019, Alabama exported $1.3 billion in forest products. From farmer to factory, many hands nurture and move these products.

This is their story, Alabama’s wood industry, men and women going out on a limb — sometimes literally.

In the world of wood, misconceptions abound. “Many people compare our trees to the rainforest or old growth,” says Ashley Smith, director of education programs for the 【47†Alabama Forestry Association†www.alaforestry.org】. “It is not true. Our climate and growth patterns are different here.” She adds that much of Alabama’s timberland has been here for years, cut for agriculture long before most of us were born.

- Sponsor -

“Our soil is fabulous for tree growth,” says Smith. Therefore, tree farms flourish. Red Hill Farm is one such fertile entity, owned by husband-and-wife team, Trice and Johnnie Nichols.

The couple has farmed their 900 acres near Prattville for about two decades, growing pine and hardwood on land that has been in Johnnie’s family since the 1850s. 

“Pines grow from seedling to 70 feet tall in 30 years,” Trice says. “A tree is similar to livestock,” he continues. “In the earlier stages of life, you ‘fatten it up,’ with plenty of water and rich soil to make the tree bigger, faster.”

Pines are rotated, thinned and sold throughout the life cycle, but as a rule, the taller the better. At its maximum height, pines reach telephone pole category — the most valuable and very marketable. Loggers take it from there.

“I love being in the woods,” says forester Earl Edmondson, of 【48†Harrison Forestry†harrisonforestry.com】/Harrison and Sons Logging in Maplesville. “The business is more mechanized now.”

His schedule is straightforward. “When the weather is dry, we haul wood.” His crews average about 156,000 tons of logs annually, spanning 22 Alabama counties.

Co-owners of Montgomery’s 【49†Legacy Land and Timber LLC†www.linkedin.com】, Bobby Loughridge and Donald Clark agree about logging’s mechanization. “Insurance companies don’t want to see us in the woods ripping trees,” Loughridge notes. “We are much less hands-on.”

In the tree business, the logger is the broker, with contracts between farmers and sawmills and factories. Once delivered, logs become raw materials and the magic happens. Alabama trees become products for the world — timber, plywood, wood pulp, paper, liner board, sawdust, poles, crossties, lumber and more.

Wood becomes commodity at the state’s major players, including 【50†Georgia-Pacific†www.gp.com】, 【51†International Paper†www.internationalpaper.com】, 【52†Packaging Corp. of America†www.packagingcorp.com】, 【53†WestRock†www.westrock.com】, 【54†Kronospan†www.kronospan-worldwide.com】, Brown-Forman Cooperage, Louisiana-Pacific, 【55†Weyerhaeuser†www.weyerhaeuser.com】, 【56†Westervelt†www.westervelt.com】 and 【57†Great Southern Wood Preserving†www.yellawood.com】.

[Image 1] Trice Nichols of Red Hill Farm.

Newer entries to the market are 【58†Rex Lumber†www.rexlumber.com】, Abbeville Fiber, 【59†Jasper Lumber†jasperlumber.com】 and Westervelt’s new Thomasville mill.

Nothing is wasted. From bark to sawdust, every component of a tree is marketable. Though each factory marches to the beat of a different saw, Alabama mills are challenged with evolving markets, increased operating costs and the erratic supply and demand issues from COVID.

“We have seen increased demand from the DIY markets in 2020 and 2021,” said Georgia-Pacific spokesperson Erica-  
Denise Solomon. “That market has pushed volume up across the board in all of our building products businesses.” GP has six facilities across Alabama.

As some markets increased, others — once staples of the industry — are dramatically shrinking. Paper, once the cornerstone of sawmills, is one such commodity. Data once written is now stored electronically. Georgia-Pacific exited the communication paper business in 2019.

Meanwhile in Abbeville, life is good for YellaWood. “We run all the time,” says Michael Lancaster, vice president of sawmill operations at Abbeville Fiber. The facility opened in summer 2019 and joins other mills supplying 15 Great Southern Wood treating plants.

“We were having a good year even before COVID,” recalls Great Southern Wood’s Ryan Blalock, chief purchasing officer. “But once the coronavirus hit, markets plunged and so did lumber supplies. But people were homebound and wanted to make improvements.”

He continues, “Suddenly, demand for YellaWood soared. We had weeks trying to supply the outrageous demand for wood.”

Today Great Southern’s supply and demand are gradually lining out but issues remain with fuel costs and staffing. “Fuel effects our loggers, truckers, suppliers, almost all phases of the business,” says Blalock. “We are seeing those costs rise dramatically.”

“Labor is also a problem,” he notes. “Fortunately, we have a group who is our backbone, but for additional growth it’s now difficult finding additional workers.”

With a January 2021 startup, one of Alabama’s newest mills is Westervelt in Thomasville, the sister plant of Westervelt in Moundville. “Production has been a struggle,” says Mark Richardson, sales and marketing director in the company’s wood products division. “We hired a full crew, but because of COVID, we were unable to conduct planned training in our Moundville plant for new Thomasville employees.”

Westervelt’s Woodlands Director Dave Donaldson adds, “I still think from a supply chain standpoint we are 18 to 24 months away (from normality). The swing may be less but we still have to deal with interruptions due to a next variant.”

Westervelt’s markets include the construction industry through building component manufacturers like truss makers, building material distribution yards and pressure treaters. 

From the newest to one of the oldest, 【60†Scotch Plywood Co†www.scotchplywood.com】.’s origins trace back to Clarke County, 1888. Today, two Alabama sites, Fulton Plywood Mill and Beatrice Mill, have a combined workforce of more than 400 employees.

“Our peak production is generally May through October,” says company Vice President Gray Skipper. “[Sales] demand goes in cycles. February through May.” He adds, “September and October are also big for us as people are rushing to make home additions, repairs and projects before winter snow hits in our Northeast and Midwest markets.”

New technologies and new uses for wood are emerging in Alabama, too, as companies create substitutes for coal. The list includes Zilkha Biomass Energy, Alabama Pellets (【61†Pinnacle Renewable Energy†www.pinnaclepellet.com】) and, coming soon to Sumter County, 【62†Enviva†www.envivabiomass.com】.

With a projected 2023 startup date, Enviva is designed to produce more than one million metric tons per year of wood pellets. The site will be the largest wood pellet production plant in the world.

“Alabama has been supportive for business and industry,” says Rick Frederick, Enviva’s Gulf Coast community relations manager. “The state provides a combination of skilled workforce, raw natural resources and tremendous terminal and port access to the Gulf, such as the 【63†Port of Mobile†www.asdd.com】. It’s a match made in heaven.”

Finally, the finished product, wood in all forms, goes to market by trucking domestically, or from tree to shining sea.

# Timber is big business in Alabama

From seeding to selling, a look at the state's forest products industry

By

【45†Emmett Burnett】

- 

January 7, 2022

[Image 0] A mix of pine and hardwood thrives on a timber farm in Alabama’s Black Belt.

I think that I shall never see, a poem as lovely as a tree. Poet Joyce Kilmer was correct. Trees are stunning, and in Alabama, lucrative.

According to the 【46†Alabama Forestry Commission†forestry.alabama.gov】’s Forest Inventory Analysis Data, the state’s 23 million acres of forested land is larger than Connecticut, Delaware, Massachusetts, New Jersey and Rhode Island combined. Approximately 93% of it is privately owned.

In 2019, Alabama exported $1.3 billion in forest products. From farmer to factory, many hands nurture and move these products.

This is their story, Alabama’s wood industry, men and women going out on a limb — sometimes literally.

In the world of wood, misconceptions abound. “Many people compare our trees to the rainforest or old growth,” says Ashley Smith, director of education programs for the 【47†Alabama Forestry Association†www.alaforestry.org】. “It is not true. Our climate and growth patterns are different here.” She adds that much of Alabama’s timberland has been here for years, cut for agriculture long before most of us were born.

- Sponsor -

“Our soil is fabulous for tree growth,” says Smith. Therefore, tree farms flourish. Red Hill Farm is one such fertile entity, owned by husband-and-wife team, Trice and Johnnie Nichols.

The couple has farmed their 900 acres near Prattville for about two decades, growing pine and hardwood on land that has been in Johnnie’s family since the 1850s. 

“Pines grow from seedling to 70 feet tall in 30 years,” Trice says. “A tree is similar to livestock,” he continues. “In the earlier stages of life, you ‘fatten it up,’ with plenty of water and rich soil to make the tree bigger, faster.”

Pines are rotated, thinned and sold throughout the life cycle, but as a rule, the taller the better. At its maximum height, pines reach telephone pole category — the most valuable and very marketable. Loggers take it from there.

“I love being in the woods,” says forester Earl Edmondson, of 【48†Harrison Forestry†harrisonforestry.com】/Harrison and Sons Logging in Maplesville. “The business is more mechanized now.”

His schedule is straightforward. “When the weather is dry, we haul wood.” His crews average about 156,000 tons of logs annually, spanning 22 Alabama counties.

Co-owners of Montgomery’s 【49†Legacy Land and Timber LLC†www.linkedin.com】, Bobby Loughridge and Donald Clark agree about logging’s mechanization. “Insurance companies don’t want to see us in the woods ripping trees,” Loughridge notes. “We are much less hands-on.”

In the tree business, the logger is the broker, with contracts between farmers and sawmills and factories. Once delivered, logs become raw materials and the magic happens. Alabama trees become products for the world — timber, plywood, wood pulp, paper, liner board, sawdust, poles, crossties, lumber and more.

Wood becomes commodity at the state’s major players, including 【50†Georgia-Pacific†www.gp.com】, 【51†International Paper†www.internationalpaper.com】, 【52†Packaging Corp. of America†www.packagingcorp.com】, 【53†WestRock†www.westrock.com】, 【54†Kronospan†www.kronospan-worldwide.com】, Brown-Forman Cooperage, Louisiana-Pacific, 【55†Weyerhaeuser†www.weyerhaeuser.com】, 【56†Westervelt†www.westervelt.com】 and 【57†Great Southern Wood Preserving†www.yellawood.com】.

[Image 1] Trice Nichols of Red Hill Farm.

Newer entries to the market are 【58†Rex Lumber†www.rexlumber.com】, Abbeville Fiber, 【59†Jasper Lumber†jasperlumber.com】 and Westervelt’s new Thomasville mill.

Nothing is wasted. From bark to sawdust, every component of a tree is marketable. Though each factory marches to the beat of a different saw, Alabama mills are challenged with evolving markets, increased operating costs and the erratic supply and demand issues from COVID.

“We have seen increased demand from the DIY markets in 2020 and 2021,” said Georgia-Pacific spokesperson Erica-  
Denise Solomon. “That market has pushed volume up across the board in all of our building products businesses.” GP has six facilities across Alabama.

As some markets increased, others — once staples of the industry — are dramatically shrinking. Paper, once the cornerstone of sawmills, is one such commodity. Data once written is now stored electronically. Georgia-Pacific exited the communication paper business in 2019.

Meanwhile in Abbeville, life is good for YellaWood. “We run all the time,” says Michael Lancaster, vice president of sawmill operations at Abbeville Fiber. The facility opened in summer 2019 and joins other mills supplying 15 Great Southern Wood treating plants.

“We were having a good year even before COVID,” recalls Great Southern Wood’s Ryan Blalock, chief purchasing officer. “But once the coronavirus hit, markets plunged and so did lumber supplies. But people were homebound and wanted to make improvements.”

He continues, “Suddenly, demand for YellaWood soared. We had weeks trying to supply the outrageous demand for wood.”

Today Great Southern’s supply and demand are gradually lining out but issues remain with fuel costs and staffing. “Fuel effects our loggers, truckers, suppliers, almost all phases of the business,” says Blalock. “We are seeing those costs rise dramatically.”

“Labor is also a problem,” he notes. “Fortunately, we have a group who is our backbone, but for additional growth it’s now difficult finding additional workers.”

With a January 2021 startup, one of Alabama’s newest mills is Westervelt in Thomasville, the sister plant of Westervelt in Moundville. “Production has been a struggle,” says Mark Richardson, sales and marketing director in the company’s wood products division. “We hired a full crew, but because of COVID, we were unable to conduct planned training in our Moundville plant for new Thomasville employees.”

Westervelt’s Woodlands Director Dave Donaldson adds, “I still think from a supply chain standpoint we are 18 to 24 months away (from normality). The swing may be less but we still have to deal with interruptions due to a next variant.”

Westervelt’s markets include the construction industry through building component manufacturers like truss makers, building material distribution yards and pressure treaters. 

From the newest to one of the oldest, 【60†Scotch Plywood Co†www.scotchplywood.com】.’s origins trace back to Clarke County, 1888. Today, two Alabama sites, Fulton Plywood Mill and Beatrice Mill, have a combined workforce of more than 400 employees.

“Our peak production is generally May through October,” says company Vice President Gray Skipper. “[Sales] demand goes in cycles. February through May.” He adds, “September and October are also big for us as people are rushing to make home additions, repairs and projects before winter snow hits in our Northeast and Midwest markets.”

New technologies and new uses for wood are emerging in Alabama, too, as companies create substitutes for coal. The list includes Zilkha Biomass Energy, Alabama Pellets (【61†Pinnacle Renewable Energy†www.pinnaclepellet.com】) and, coming soon to Sumter County, 【62†Enviva†www.envivabiomass.com】.

With a projected 2023 startup date, Enviva is designed to produce more than one million metric tons per year of wood pellets. The site will be the largest wood pellet production plant in the world.

“Alabama has been supportive for business and industry,” says Rick Frederick, Enviva’s Gulf Coast community relations manager. “The state provides a combination of skilled workforce, raw natural resources and tremendous terminal and port access to the Gulf, such as the 【63†Port of Mobile†www.asdd.com】. It’s a match made in heaven.”

Finally, the finished product, wood in all forms, goes to market by trucking domestically, or from tree to shining sea.

metadata.text:
A Bureau of Reclamation (Reclamation) lease of power privilege (LOPP) is a contractual right given to a non-federal entity to use a Reclamation asset (e.g. dam or conduit) for electric power generation consistent with Reclamation project purposes. A LOPP project must not impair the efficiency of Reclamation generated power or water deliveries, jeopardize public safety, or negatively affect any other Reclamation project purpose. 

#### Non-Federal Hydroelectric Power Development

Both Reclamation and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) are authorized to permit the use of Reclamation assets to non-federal entities for the purposes of hydropower development – Reclamation via a LOPP and FERC via a 【51†License†www.ferc.gov】. In the interest of mutual cooperation for the timely development of non-federal hydropower, the two agencies have collaborated to define jurisdictional boundaries and responsibilities. The outcomes of this collaboration are memorialized in two Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) agreements. Per the MoU documents, each Reclamation asset is subject to only one permitting process; non-federal entities seeking to utilize a Reclamation asset for the purposes of hydropower development would be required to obtain either a Reclamation LOPP or FERC License – but not both.

Date Memorandum of Understanding Purpose  
1981 【52†MoU between the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission of the Department of Energy and the Water and Power Resources Service (Reclamation) of the Department of the Interior】 MoU establishes a process to promote the non-Federal development of hydroelectric energy at existing Water and Power (Reclamation) facilities.  
1992 【53†MoU between the Federal Regulatory Commission and the Department of the Interior, Bureau of Reclamation】 MoU establishes procedural steps and a set of rebuttable presumptions to guide the analysis of the agencies' respective jurisdiction over hydro development at Reclamation sites.  

The general premise of the MoU agreements is that - unless otherwise specified in law - Reclamation assets authorized for federal hydropower development are within the exclusive jurisdiction of Reclamation – and require a LOPP for non-federal development. All other Reclamation assets (i.e. assets not authorized for federal hydropower development) are within the exclusive jurisdiction of FERC – and require a FERC License for non-federal development. Non-federal hydropower projects developed on Reclamation projects typically utilize one of two Reclamation asset types – (1) conduits or (2) dams (and associated reservoirs).

  1. Pursuant to the Reclamation Project Act of 1939 (Public Law 76-260), as amended by the 【54†Bureau of Reclamation Small Conduit Hydropower Development and Rural Jobs Act of 2013】 (Public Law 113-24), all Reclamation conduits are within the exclusive jurisdiction of Reclamation. Therefore, all non-federal hydropower development utilizing a Reclamation conduit would proceed through a LOPP. 
  2. Per the MoU, the utilization of Reclamation dams for non-federal hydropower development requires either a LOPP or FERC License – dependent upon the authorized purpose of the utilized dam. As with all Reclamation assets, permitting authority is mutually exclusive; each Reclamation dam is either within Reclamation or FERC jurisdiction. Accordingly, development would proceed through either a LOPP or FERC License - but not both. 

Note that comprehensive, non-federal projects utilizing multiple assets may require both a LOPP and FERC License in the circumstance that one asset is within Reclamation’s jurisdiction and a second asset is within FERC’s jurisdiction. This circumstance may apply to non-federal pumped storage projects utilizing a Reclamation dam authorized for federal hydropower development and any second dam (Reclamation-owned or otherwise) within FERC’s jurisdiction.   

Finally - Section 3087 of the 【55†Carl Levin and Howard P. "Buck" McKeon National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2015】 (Public Law 113-291) authorizes the issuance of LOPPs on all water resource assets constructed pursuant to the Water Conservation and Utilization Act (WCUA) (Public Law 76-398), therefore, all non-federal hydropower utilizing WCUA assets would proceed exclusively through a LOPP. 

#### Initiating Non-Federal Development

To initiate non-federal hydropower development on a Reclamation conduit or WCUA asset, developers are instructed to submit a Formal Request to the appropriate Reclamation Regional Director. Once the Formal Request is received, the developer will be notified and the project will proceed through the LOPP process. To initiate non-federal hydropower development on a Reclamation dam, developers are instructed to submit either a Formal Request to the appropriate Reclamation Regional Director or a Notice of Intent to FERC. Developers are free to choose which agency to contact. Once the Formal Request or Notice of Intent is received, the two agencies will convene to determine the appropriate permitting authority. Once the appropriate permitting authority is determined, the developer will be notified and the project will proceed through the appropriate permitting process(es).

The Southeastern Power Administration (SEPA) is a body that oversees hydropower operations in the southeastern region of the United States. While it may not have a program identical to the Lease of Power Privilege (LOPP) of the Bureau of Reclamation, it does play a crucial role in managing and marketing hydropower from federal water projects in this region. The Department of Energy, through SEPA, works alongside entities such as the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Bureau of Reclamation, International Boundary and Water Commission, and Tennessee Valley Authority in ensuring the generation and distribution of hydropower. Federal dams in the U.S., including those in the southeastern region, have a total capacity of 42-gigawatts for hydropower generation【32†source】.

The SEPA operates within a network of high voltage transmission lines to deliver electricity generated at federal dams to the public. The hydropower facilities could be of various types including impoundment hydropower which uses a dam to store water, diversion hydropower which channels a portion of a river, or pumped storage which moves water between reservoirs at different elevations based on electricity demand.

For more specific programs or arrangements akin to LOPP in the southeastern U.S., contacting local or federal energy authorities or the Southeastern Power Administration directly might provide the precise information.

Electricity produced at Federal dams plays a critical role to meeting everyday energy needs of Americans. The dams, owned by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Bureau of Reclamation, International Boundary and Water Commission and Tennessee Valley Authority serve many other important roles. Federal dams have a 42-gigawatt capacity.

### Comprehensive Report: Carbon Sequestration and Regulatory Compliance

#### Introduction

This report investigates the process of carbon sequestration in forestry, its application for shippers and the aviation industry, and relevant regulatory frameworks. The goal is to provide a detailed understanding of how carbon sequestration can be leveraged for emission reductions and cost management, and to clarify the regulatory landscape, specifically in the EU and IMO contexts.

#### Carbon Sequestration in Forestry

**Process of Carbon Sequestration**

- **Mechanism**: Carbon sequestration in forestry involves capturing and storing atmospheric CO2 in trees and soil through photosynthesis.
- **Components**: 
  - Above-ground biomass (trunks, branches, leaves)
  - Below-ground biomass (roots)
  - Soil organic matter

**Calculation of CO2 Stored**

- **Methods**:
  - **Allometric Equations**: Used to estimate tree biomass based on diameter at breast height (DBH) and tree height.
  - **Forest Inventory Data**: Collection of tree measurements, species composition, and stand density.
- **Conversion**:
  - Biomass to Carbon: 50% of dry biomass is typically carbon.
  - Carbon to CO2 Equivalent: Multiply by 44/12 (molecular weight ratio of CO2 to carbon).

**Conversion into Certificates for Sale**

- **Verification**: Third-party verification of carbon sequestration claims.
- **Standards**: Compliance with standards such as Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) or Gold Standard.
- **Marketplaces**: Platforms like the American Carbon Registry (ACR) facilitate the trade of carbon credits.

#### Regulatory Compliance: EU and IMO Regulations

**EU Regulations on Carbon Offsetting**

- **Current Framework**:
  - **EU ETS**: The EU Emissions Trading System does not permit the use of carbon offsetting to replace EU ETS certificates in the maritime sector.
  - **Directive (EU) 2018/410**: Strengthens the EU ETS by eliminating the use of international carbon credits within the system.
  - **MARPOL Annex VI and MRV Regulation**: Mandate strict monitoring, reporting, and verification of CO2 emissions.

- **Rationale**:
  - **Environmental Integrity**: Ensures genuine emission reductions within the EU ETS framework.
  - **Market Stability**: Prevents market distortions and maintains the effectiveness of the cap-and-trade system.

**IMO Regulations on Carbon Offsetting**

- **Current Stance**:
  - The IMO does not allow carbon offsetting to replace mandatory certificates. The focus is on improving energy efficiency and reducing emissions directly through measures such as EEDI and SEEMP.
- **Future Considerations**:
  - **Market-Based Measures (MBMs)**: Under discussion as part of the IMO's GHG strategy, potentially including carbon pricing or trading schemes.
  - **2023 Revision**: The IMO is scheduled to review its GHG strategy, which may include new mechanisms for emission reductions.

#### Benefits of Carbon Sequestration for Shippers and Aviation

**Current and Potential Benefits**

- **Regulatory Compliance**:
  - **Offsetting Emissions**: Helps meet regulatory requirements and enhance sustainability profiles.
  - **Cost Management**: Provides a cost-effective way to meet emissions reduction targets.

- **Operational Benefits**:
  - **Brand Enhancement**: Enhances reputation and customer loyalty.
  - **Investment Attraction**: Attracts sustainable and ethical investments.

**Reduction of Carbon Exposure and Costs**

- **Economic Viability**: Forestry-based carbon credits are often cost-effective.
- **Long-term Benefits**: Ensures sustained compliance and financial incentives, such as tax benefits and green financing.

**Examples and Case Studies**

- **Delta Air Lines**: Invested in reforestation projects in the Mississippi Valley to offset emissions.
- **Maersk**: Explored afforestation projects to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050.
- **United Airlines**: Invested in forest conservation and restoration projects in Brazil.

#### Conclusion

Carbon sequestration via forestry offers significant benefits for shippers and the aviation industry, including regulatory compliance, cost management, and enhanced sustainability profiles. Both the EU and IMO have stringent regulations to ensure direct emission reductions, though the IMO is exploring market-based measures for future implementation. Companies like Delta Air Lines, Maersk, and United Airlines exemplify the practical benefits of engaging in carbon sequestration projects.

### Investigation: EU Regulation on Carbon Offsetting in the Maritime Sector

#### Confirmation of EU Regulation

- **EU ETS and Maritime Sector**:
  - **Regulation**: The EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) is the cornerstone of the EU’s policy to combat climate change and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
  - **Maritime Sector**: As of the latest regulations, the EU does not permit the use of carbon offsetting to replace EU ETS certificates in the maritime sector.

- **Directive (EU) 2018/410**: 
  - **Amendment to EU ETS**: This directive reinforces the restriction by updating and strengthening the EU ETS framework, emphasizing the need for direct emission reductions rather than reliance on offsets.

#### Specific Regulations and Guidelines

- **Relevant Legislation**:
  - **Directive (EU) 2018/410**: Amending Directive 2003/87/EC to enhance cost-effective emission reductions and low-carbon investments.
  - **Regulation (EU) 2015/757**: On the monitoring, reporting, and verification of CO2 emissions from maritime transport (MRV Regulation).

- **Key Provisions**:
  - **EU ETS Directive (2003/87/EC)**: Establishes a cap-and-trade system where shipping companies must hold sufficient allowances to cover their verified emissions.
  - **Amendment (Directive 2018/410)**: Strengthens the EU ETS by reducing the overall number of allowances and eliminating the use of international carbon credits (offsets) within the system.
  - **MRV Regulation**: Requires ship owners to monitor and report CO2 emissions for vessels above 5,000 gross tonnage calling at EU ports, forming the basis for inclusion in the EU ETS.

- **Guidelines and Implementation**:
  - **Monitoring and Reporting**: Ships must adhere to strict monitoring, reporting, and verification processes to quantify CO2 emissions.
  - **Compliance**: Shipping companies must ensure they have enough EU ETS allowances to cover their annual emissions, promoting direct emission reductions rather than relying on offsets.

- **Rationale for Exclusion of Offsets**:
  - **Environmental Integrity**: The exclusion of offsets ensures that emissions reductions are genuine and occur within the sectors covered by the EU ETS.
  - **Market Stability**: Prevents potential market distortions and maintains the effectiveness of the cap-and-trade system by ensuring emissions reductions are real and measurable.

#### Summary

The EU's regulatory framework explicitly prohibits the use of carbon offsetting to replace EU ETS certificates in the maritime sector. This is enforced through Directive (EU) 2018/410, which amends the original EU ETS Directive to strengthen the system and eliminate the use of international offsets. The MRV Regulation further supports this by mandating rigorous CO2 emissions monitoring and reporting for ships. These measures ensure that emission reductions are direct and verifiable, maintaining the integrity and effectiveness of the EU ETS.

  - **MARPOL Annex VI**: The primary regulation addressing air pollution from ships, including energy efficiency measures such as the Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI) and the Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP).

- **Current Stance**:

- **Future Considerations**:
  - **Market-Based Measures (MBMs)**: The IMO is considering various market-based measures as part of its long-term strategy to reduce GHG emissions, which may include carbon pricing or trading schemes. However, these measures are still under discussion and have not been formally adopted.

### Investigation: Carbon Sequestration in Forestry

#### 1. Process of Carbon Sequestration in Forestry
Carbon sequestration in forestry involves capturing and storing atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) in trees, plants, and soil. The process includes:
- **Photosynthesis**: Trees and plants absorb CO2 from the atmosphere and convert it into organic matter through photosynthesis, storing carbon in their biomass (trunks, branches, leaves, and roots).
- **Growth and Accumulation**: As trees grow, they accumulate more carbon in their biomass. The carbon remains stored as long as the trees are alive and growing.
- **Soil Storage**: Fallen leaves, branches, and roots contribute to soil organic matter, which also stores carbon over long periods.

#### 2. Calculating CO2 Stored in Trees
Timberland owners calculate the amount of CO2 stored in trees using several methods, including:
- **Tree Measurements**: Measuring tree diameter, height, and species to estimate biomass. Common tools include diameter tape, clinometers, and allometric equations.
- **Biomass Equations**: Applying species-specific biomass equations to convert tree measurements into estimates of above-ground and below-ground biomass.
- **Carbon Conversion Factors**: Using established carbon conversion factors (e.g., 50% of dry biomass is carbon) to estimate the amount of carbon stored.
- **Growth Models**: Employing forest growth models and inventory data to project future carbon sequestration.

#### 3. Conversion into Certificates for Sale
The calculated CO2 storage is converted into carbon certificates through a standardized process:
- **Verification and Certification**: Independent verification bodies assess the accuracy of carbon sequestration calculations and ensure compliance with established standards (e.g., Verified Carbon Standard (VCS), Gold Standard).
- **Issuance of Certificates**: Verified carbon sequestration amounts are converted into carbon credits or certificates, typically measured in metric tons of CO2 equivalent (tCO2e).
- **Registry and Trading**: Carbon credits are registered in official registries (e.g., VCS Registry, Gold Standard Registry) and can be sold or traded in carbon markets. Buyers, such as companies or individuals aiming to offset their carbon footprint, purchase these certificates.

#### Example:
- **Measurement**: A timberland owner measures a forest plot and determines the biomass using tree measurements and allometric equations.
- **Calculation**: The biomass is converted to carbon content using conversion factors. For instance, if a plot contains 100 tons of biomass, it stores approximately 50 tons of carbon.
- **Certification**: An independent verifier confirms the calculations and compliance with standards. The verified amount (e.g., 50 tons of carbon or 183.3 tCO2e) is issued as carbon credits.
- **Sale**: These credits are listed in a carbon registry and made available for sale to entities looking to offset their emissions.

#### Research the Process of Carbon Sequestration in Forestry

- **Definition and Mechanism:**
  - **Carbon Sequestration**: The process by which forests absorb CO2 from the atmosphere through photosynthesis and store it as carbon in biomass (trees, vegetation) and soil.
  - **Biomass Components**: Includes above-ground (trunks, branches, leaves) and below-ground (roots) biomass.

- **Carbon Cycle in Forests:**
  - **Photosynthesis**: Trees absorb CO2 and convert it into organic matter.
  - **Carbon Storage**: Stored in living biomass, dead organic matter (fallen leaves, dead trees), and soil organic matter.
  - **Decomposition**: Releases stored carbon back into the atmosphere; however, sustainable forest management can enhance net carbon storage.

- **Forest Management Practices:**
  - **Reforestation**: Planting trees on degraded land.
  - **Afforestation**: Establishing forests on non-forested land.
  - **Sustainable Logging**: Harvesting trees in a manner that maintains forest carbon stocks.

#### Calculation of CO2 Stored in Trees by Timberland Owners

- **Methods and Tools:**
  - **Allometric Equations**: Mathematical models that estimate tree biomass based on measurable parameters like diameter at breast height (DBH) and tree height.
  - **Forest Inventory Data**: Periodic measurement of tree dimensions, species composition, and stand density.

- **Steps to Calculate CO2 Storage:**
  1. **Measure Tree Dimensions**: DBH, height, and species identification.
  2. **Estimate Biomass**: Use allometric equations to calculate the biomass of individual trees.
  3. **Calculate Carbon Content**: Biomass is converted to carbon content (typically, 50% of dry biomass is carbon).
  4. **Convert to CO2 Equivalent**: Multiply the carbon content by the molecular weight ratio of CO2 to carbon (44/12) to obtain the amount of CO2 sequestered.

- **Technology and Software:**
  - **GIS and Remote Sensing**: Mapping and monitoring forest cover and biomass.
  - **Carbon Accounting Tools**: Software like COMET-Farm and CBM-CFS3 for comprehensive carbon assessments.

#### Conversion of CO2 Calculations into Certificates for Sale

- **Certification Process:**
  - **Verification**: Third-party organizations verify the carbon sequestration claims through field assessments and data analysis.
  - **Standards and Protocols**: Compliance with recognized standards such as Verified Carbon Standard (VCS), Climate Action Reserve (CAR), or Gold Standard.
  - **Issuance of Certificates**: Verified CO2 sequestration is converted into carbon credits or certificates, representing a quantifiable amount of CO2 removed from the atmosphere.

- **Market Dynamics:**
  - **Buyers and Sellers**: Companies seeking to offset their emissions purchase these certificates from timberland owners or forest project developers.
  - **Carbon Marketplaces**: Platforms like the American Carbon Registry (ACR) and Carbon Trade Exchange (CTX) facilitate the buying and selling of carbon credits.
  - **Price Determinants**: Market demand, certification standards, and the credibility of the sequestration project influence certificate prices.

#### Summary

The process of carbon sequestration in forestry involves the absorption and storage of CO2 in tree biomass and soil. Timberland owners calculate the CO2 stored using allometric equations and forest inventory data, which is then converted into CO2 equivalents. These calculations undergo third-party verification and are issued as certificates or carbon credits, which can be sold in carbon markets. Sustainable forest management practices play a crucial role in maintaining and enhancing carbon stocks, contributing to climate change mitigation efforts.

Alright, Captain, let's dive into call options in the stock market.

A call option is a financial contract that gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy a stock at a specified price (the strike price) within a certain time period. Here's how it works:

1. **Buy a Call Option**: You buy a call option on a stock if you anticipate the stock price will rise before the expiration date of the option.
2. **Strike Price**: This is the price at which you can buy the stock. It's set when you buy the option.
3. **Expiration Date**: The option has a specific date by which you must decide to use it or let it expire.
4. **Premium**: This is the cost of the option, which you pay to the seller.

If the stock price rises above the strike price before the expiration, you can exercise the option to buy the stock at the lower strike price and potentially sell it at a higher market price, making a profit. If the stock price doesn't rise as expected, you can let the option expire, losing only the premium paid.

The length of an option, also known as its expiration term, is determined by the specific terms set when the option is created. Options can have various expiration lengths, typically ranging from a week to several years. The most common durations are:

- **Short-term options**: These usually expire within a year and are often used for more immediate trading strategies.
- **Long-term options**: Known as LEAPS (Long-Term Equity Anticipation Securities), these can have expiration dates up to three years in the future, appealing to investors with a longer-term outlook.

The expiration length is an essential factor in options trading, as it influences the option's value and the strategy employed by the trader. Longer-term options generally have higher premiums due to the extended opportunity for the underlying asset to move in a favorable direction.

The length of an option, known as its expiration period, is determined by the specific terms set when the option is created. The expiration date is a key aspect of an option's contract and is agreed upon by the buyer and seller at the time of the option's purchase. A classic critical thinking puzzle is the "Monty Hall Problem." Here's how it goes: 

You're on a game show and given the choice of three doors. Behind one door is a car, behind the others, goats. You pick a door, say No. 1, and the host, who knows what's behind the doors, opens another door, say No. 3, which has a goat. He then asks if you want to stick with your original choice or switch to the remaining unopened door.

This famous problem often describes a situation where you start at the North Pole. If you start at the North Pole, walking one mile south takes you into a latitude slightly away from the pole. Walking one mile west from there won’t affect your position much because you're circling around near the pole. Then, walking one mile north would take you back to the North Pole.

Interestingly, this can also happen at some specific points near the South Pole. These points allow you to walk one mile south to a latitude where the circumference of the circle is exactly one mile. Walking one mile west would make a full circle around the Earth at that latitude, and walking one mile north would take you back to the starting point. These points would be just over a mile north of the latitude where the Earth's circumference is one mile.

"Our 2021 financial performance was the strongest on record and each of our businesses delivered exceptional results despite persistent operational and market challenges," said Devin W. Stockfish, president and chief executive officer. "Our teams delivered the highest Wood Products Adjusted EBITDA on record, captured over $70 million of operational excellence improvements, optimized our timberlands holdings through strategic transactions in Alabama and Washington, and launched our new Natural Climate Solutions business. As we enter 2022, we continue to be encouraged by strong demand fundamentals that will drive growth for our businesses and remain focused on creating superior value for shareholders through our unmatched portfolio of assets, industry-leading operating performance, strong ESG foundation and disciplined capital allocation."

Adjusted FAD measures cash generated during the period (net of capital expenditures and significant non-recurring items) that is available for dividends, repurchases of common shares, debt reduction, acquisitions, and other discretionary and nondiscretionary capital allocation activities. Adjusted FAD should not be considered in isolation from, and is not intended to represent an alternative to, our GAAP results. Adjusted FAD measures cash generated during the period (net of capital expenditures and significant non-recurring items) that is available for dividends, repurchases of common shares, debt reduction, acquisitions, and other discretionary and nondiscretionary capital allocation activities. Adjusted FAD should not be considered in isolation from, and is not intended to represent an alternative to, our GAAP results. A reconciliation of Adjusted FAD to net cash from operations is included within this release.

West Fraser Timber Co. Ltd., commonly known as "West Fraser", is a Canadian 【57†forestry company】 that produces lumber, 【58†laminated veneer lumber】 (LVL), 【59†medium-density fibreboard】 (MDF), 【60†oriented strand board】 (OSB), plywood, pulp, newsprint, and wood chips.[2] Based in 【61†Vancouver】, 【51†British Columbia】, the company is a member of the 【62†Forest Products Association of Canada】.[3] As of 2023【29†[update]】, West Fraser had been recognized eight times as one of Canada's Top 100 Employers.[4]

## History[【63†edit】]

West Fraser Timber was founded in 1955 by three brothers from Seattle: Samuel Kendall Ketcham, Henry Holman ("Pete") Ketcham Jr., and William Peters Ketcham.[5] Their father was 【64†Hank Ketcham】, who played 【65†college football】 for the 【66†Yale Bulldogs】 and was inducted to the 【67†College Football Hall of Fame】.[6]

The three brothers decided to do business together and purchased a small planing mill in 【50†Quesnel, British Columbia】. Samual Ketcham served as president of the company until his death in November 1977 in a helicopter crash.[7] He was succeeded by Douglas Johnston,[8] and later by Chester Johnson. 【54†Henry H. Ketcham】, son of "Pete" Ketcham, became president in 1985.[9] He led the company through an 【68†initial public offering】 in May 1986.[10] Later, Ketcham also became CEO and oversaw the company until 2012.[11] Ted Seraphim subsequently became president and then CEO,[12] until being succeeded by Raymond Ferris as president in April 2018 and CEO in June 2019.[13]

As of 2018, "West Fraser has become the largest lumber manufacturer in North America with 8,600 employees globally – about 5,000 in Western Canada – at about 50 locations."[4]

In April 2020, it was revealed that Canadian business magnate 【69†Jim Pattison】 had upped his stake in West Fraser to 13.8% ownership, prompting speculation that the billionaire had plans to merge the company with 【70†Canfor】, of which he owns 51%. In response, West Fraser adopted a 【71†shareholder rights plan】 or "poison pill" in order to defend against any attempts at a 【72†takeover】.[14][15]

### Who Is BFGoodrich?

BFGoodrich has a long and rich history, they are one of the most trusted brands for tires because of this. They have had the time and expertise to perfect their tire-creation process. They began way back in 1870.

### Why Is The KO2 So Great?

The KO2 is a very commonly chosen tire because of its fantastic price point as well as its overall reliability and safety. When you break it all down, your tires should be the most practical aftermarket purchase that you make. You want a tire that will be long lasting, durable, and reliable while giving you a great driving experience.

Since this is an all-terrain tire, it isn't the most aggressive or stylish tire on the market. If you are looking strictly for aesthetics then this tire might not be for you. If you just want a really great all-around tire for both on and off the road, then look no further.

This KO2 is raved about by everyone and truly is a great tire for any usage you may have. On-road it is quiet and comfortable, and off-road it has great grip and traction. In wet, dry, and snowy conditions, the KO2 is known for its insane traction.

On top of all of that, it has a long tread life so you will get thousands upon thousands of miles out of this tire. It is also very durable, so you don't need to worry about getting a flat. We really can't find much that we don't like about the BFGoodrich KO2.

### Key Features:

  * CoreGard Technology that increases sidewall strength by 20%
  * Awesome performance in dry, wet, or snowy conditions thanks to a serrated shoulder design
  * 50,000 mile manufacturer’s treadwear warranty
  * Quiet and comfortable ride

### Who Is BFGoodrich?

BFGoodrich has a long and rich history, they are one of the most trusted brands for tires because of this. They have had the time and expertise to perfect their tire-creation process. They began way back in 1870.

### Why Is The KO2 So Great?

The KO2 is a very commonly chosen tire because of its fantastic price point as well as its overall reliability and safety. When you break it all down, your tires should be the most practical aftermarket purchase that you make. You want a tire that will be long lasting, durable, and reliable while giving you a great driving experience.

Since this is an all-terrain tire, it isn't the most aggressive or stylish tire on the market. If you are looking strictly for aesthetics then this tire might not be for you. If you just want a really great all-around tire for both on and off the road, then look no further.

This KO2 is raved about by everyone and truly is a great tire for any usage you may have. On-road it is quiet and comfortable, and off-road it has great grip and traction. In wet, dry, and snowy conditions, the KO2 is known for its insane traction.

On top of all of that, it has a long tread life so you will get thousands upon thousands of miles out of this tire. It is also very durable, so you don't need to worry about getting a flat. We really can't find much that we don't like about the BFGoodrich KO2.

### Key Features:

  * CoreGard Technology that increases sidewall strength by 20%
  * Awesome performance in dry, wet, or snowy conditions thanks to a serrated shoulder design
  * 50,000 mile manufacturer’s treadwear warranty
  * Quiet and comfortable ride

Here are three options for purchasing 315/70R17 BF Goodrich KO2 tires in the Nashville, TN area, including onsite mount and balance services:

1. **Discount Tire - Nashville, TN**
   - **Price:** Approximately $276 per tire, plus additional costs for mount and balance.
   - **Address:** 3423 Gallatin Pike, Nashville, TN 37216
   - **Phone Number:** (615) 226-0110
   - **Details:** Discount Tire offers onsite mount and balance services. They have a good reputation for competitive pricing and quality service, including a 90-day price match guarantee.

2. **4 Wheel Parts - Nashville, TN**
   - **Price:** $395.57 per tire
   - **Address:** 515 W Thompson Ln, Nashville, TN 37211
   - **Phone Number:** (615) 832-0888
   - **Details:** 4 Wheel Parts offers professional onsite mount and balance services. They provide a comprehensive service experience, including free in-store pickup and the ability to schedule an installation appointment.

3. **Firestone Complete Auto Care - Nashville, TN**
   - **Price:** Approximately $300 per tire, depending on promotions and additional services.
   - **Address:** 2412 West End Ave, Nashville, TN 37203
   - **Phone Number:** (615) 320-9117
   - **Details:** Firestone Complete Auto Care provides onsite mount and balance services, often with various promotional offers. They have a well-established reputation for tire service and maintenance.

These vendors provide onsite mount and balance services, ensuring that you can purchase and have your tires professionally installed all in one place.

I reviewed the pricing for the other two recommendations:

1. **4 Wheel Parts - Nashville, TN**
   - **Current Price:** $395.57 per tire
   - **Address:** 515 W Thompson Ln, Nashville, TN 37211
   - **Phone Number:** (615) 832-0888
   - **Details:** 4 Wheel Parts does offer the BF Goodrich KO2 at $395.57 per tire, with onsite mount and balance services available. This price is up-to-date and verified【27†source】【28†source】.

2. **Firestone Complete Auto Care - Nashville, TN**
   - **Current Price:** Approximately $300 per tire (depending on specific promotions)
   - **Address:** 2412 West End Ave, Nashville, TN 37203
   - **Phone Number:** (615) 320-9117
   - **Details:** Firestone’s pricing can vary based on current promotions and specific tire models. It's advisable to check with them directly for the most accurate quote for the BF Goodrich KO2 tires.

If you need further assistance or additional options, feel free to ask!

Fortum is a Finnish energy company that operates in various parts of the energy sector, including electricity generation, heat production, and related services. They have a strong focus on sustainable energy solutions, particularly in the areas of hydroelectric, nuclear, and renewable energy sources like wind and solar. Fortum operates mainly in the Nordic and Baltic countries, Russia, Poland, and India.

What's your next move regarding Fortum?
who is fortum

summarize the following

Call with Fortum 18th Oct
Juha Sainio
Tom Backman

They see demand increasing over the coming years due to decarbonisation.

By 2030 could see 500 TWh a year demand which could double by 2050.

Fortum have around 1 GW of renewable capacity under permitting in Finland. After permitting is confirmed they would want to confirm off takers. 

Fortum will use the Hydro production to fill in the intermittent supply wind and solar in order to provide renewable Baseload.

Providing baseload pricing is not an issue unless production of renewables and production of hydrogen need to be assessed on an hourly basis. We need to look into this in more detail and Juha soar they would introduce us to their team responsible for  regulation.  

They mentioned no Finnish suppliers  are/can currently offer baseload supply of renewables. 

Although the 10yr market price is showing a price around €44/MWh, they do not believe this is a true reflection of the market (lack of liquidity). Tom believes prices will move more towards the cost of new capacity. They also seem to believe that prices may be higher in future due to demand requirements. 

They are pricing a 10yr PPA around €53.25/MWh which does not include FINGRID transmission costs.

For Guarantee of Origin (from wind or solar) it is a further €5.50/MWh. 

The Guarantee of Origin is a European market price. To me this sounds very similar to a Renewable Energy Certificate in the US, where you can buy a Guarantee of Orgin and use it to show you have used renewable energy that has been produced in Europe. 
However, it sounds that the Guarantee of origin will not be valid for the production of Green Hydrogen as you need to generate the renewable energy in the location you are producing the hydrogen. 

A point we will need to clear here is this is the same for the US? Can we only produce green hydrogen in locations where the renewables is available? 

They will revert back with comments on the NDA and we can discuss our requirements in more detail. They will also introduce to their team responsible for regulations.

Call with Fortum Summary:

- Demand expected to rise due to decarbonization; 500 TWh/year by 2030, potentially double by 2050.
- Fortum has 1 GW renewable capacity under permitting in Finland. Looking for off takers post-permit.
- Hydro production will supplement intermittent wind and solar to provide renewable baseload.
- No Finnish suppliers currently offer baseload supply of renewables.
- Current 10-yr market price around €44/MWh is not reflective of real market; Fortum estimates around €53.25/MWh without transmission costs.
- Additional €5.50/MWh for Guarantee of Origin, similar to Renewable Energy Certificates in the US. Not valid for green hydrogen production.
- Follow-ups include clarification on NDA and introduction to their regulations team.

🧑‍💼: Filing as 'Head of Household' is a tax filing status in the U.S. It's for individuals who are unmarried and have paid more than half the cost of maintaining a home for a year. This home must also be the main home for a qualifying person, like a dependent child or relative.

To determine if you should file under this status because someone lives with you, here are the key questions:
1. Are you unmarried or considered unmarried at the end of the tax year?

### Total biofuel production growth by region, main case, 2021-2027

### Total biofuel production by feedstock, main case, 2021-2027

【103† Open expand 】 

* * *

#### Four regions are driving demand

The United States, Europe, Brazil and Indonesia are responsible for the majority of biodiesel, renewable diesel and biojet fuel consumption growth. Combined, demand for these fuels increases by 44% or 21 billion litres in our main case over 2022-2027. In the United States, the renewable fuel standard, state-level low-carbon fuel standards and the IRA’s tax credits boost demand for renewable diesel and biojet fuel. Most requirements are met with domestic production from a mixture of feedstocks (e.g. soybean oil, rapeseed oil, corn oil, used cooking oil and animal fats). 

In Europe also, consumption of renewable diesel and biojet fuel increase the most. Total demand growth is relatively small, but the European Union is phasing out the use of palm oil and has placed limits on other feedstocks, which is boosting production from wastes, residues and rapeseed oil. Meanwhile, Brazil and Indonesia both have biodiesel blending mandates that will become more stringent over the forecast period. Indonesian biofuel manufacturers primarily use palm oil to produce biodiesel, and Brazilian ones rely on soybean oil.   

* * *

#### The looming supply crunch…

Consumption of vegetable oil for biofuel production is expected to increase 46% to 54 million tonnes over 2022-2027, raising the share of vegetable oil production directed to meeting growing biofuel demand from 17% to 23%. In the United States, this increase in demand is already reducing 【104†soybean oil export†www.usda.gov】 estimates and supporting 【105†higher prices†apps.fas.usda.gov】. 

Used cooking oil and animal fats are unlikely to provide relief, as they are in even higher demand because they offer lower GHG emissions intensity and meet EU feedstock requirements. In fact, the use of used cooking oil and animal fats nearly exhausts 100% of estimated supplies over the forecast period. Even when a broader range of wastes (such as palm oil mill effluent, tall oil and other agribusiness waste oils) is considered, demand still swells to nearly 65% of global supply.   

### Biofuel demand share of global wastes and residues, main case, 2010-2027

【106† Open expand 】 

### Biofuel demand share of global crop production, main case, 2010-2027

【107† Open expand 】 

* * *

If this situation remains unchanged throughout the forecast period, the potential for biofuels to contribute to global decarbonisation efforts could be undermined. Bio-based diesel and biokerosene are essential components of net zero pathways because they can be used in marine, aviation and heavy trucking applications, for which few other decarbonisation options exist. However, attaining a 【108†net zero trajectory】 would require a more than three times production increase in our main case.   

* * *

#### … and how it may be avoided

Our forecast takes a relatively static view of agricultural and waste oil markets. This doesn’t Steep prices will prompt companies and governments to improve feedstock supply chains, seek out new supplies and develop new techniques. 

Policies and programmes in the United States, Canada and Europe will be helpful. In the United States, the 【109†Sustainable Aviation Grand Challenge Roadmap†www.energy.gov】 aims to improve understanding of the feedstock challenge, boost supply potential and support new technology development. Meanwhile, the European Union as a whole, and individual member states such as Germany, have dedicated targets for fuels made from less-developed wastes and residues. In Canada, a USD 1.1‑billion 【110†Clean Fuels Fund†www.nrcan.gc.ca】 supports supply chain development. Policies focused on GHG emissions reductions can also be useful, since they give biofuel producers an incentive to reduce the GHG intensity of their fuels, not just produce more. This can mean lower feedstock requirements with the same or better GHG emissions benefit. 

Biofuel producers and users are also interested in expanding feedstock supplies for commercial biofuel technologies, as additional stocks could support up to another 8.5 EJ of biofuel production (300 billion litres), compared with 4 EJ (160 billion litres) in 2021 (see table below for sources). The industry sector is also investing in new technologies that use more widely available feedstocks, offering up to 50 EJ of sustainable potential. In fact, expanding commercial and new technologies could sustainably 【111†increase bio-based diesel and biokerosene production†iea.blob.core.windows.net】 more than four times by 2030. 

Exploiting the potential of conventional crop-based feedstocks that meet sustainability requirements could support a near-【112†70% increase in biofuel production†iea.blob.core.windows.net】 by 2030 from the 2021 level. Although there are limits to the pace and scale of growth for certain feedstocks such as vegetable oils, crops already support a 20% increase in liquid biofuel production by 2027 in the main-case forecast.
