The properties evaluated during the course of this trial were limited to: bending strength and stiffness, 
internal bond and thickness swelling.  Flatwise bending strength was evaluated in accordance with the 
third point loading method described in ASTM D4761 (Figure 18).  Internal bond and thickness swelling 
were evaluated in accordance with ASTM D1037 test methods. 
 
 
 

 
Figure 18 Third point loading test on short beam 
 
 
A total of 42 aspen specimens were tested in flatwise bending. Specimens were not conditioned prior to 
testing. It should be noted that changes in density, resin content and press cycles were made during the 
course of the experimentation in order to get the maximum amount of information on the optimal process 
conditions.  Therefore, the coefficients of variation observed during these tests should not be considered 
as representative of “normal” operating conditions. 
 
Table 2 provides a summary of all test results on aspen billets.  At an average density of 45 lb/ft3 , the 
average modulus of rupture (MOR) was  8,840 psi and the average modulus of elasticity was 2,2 million 
psi.  This compares favourably to the properties of aspen LVL.  Based on these test results, a MOE of 2.0 
million psi would be expected at a density of 40 lb/ft3 . Thickness swell values were relatively low at 7 
percent.

A total of 90 birch specimens were tested in flatwise bending.  At an average density of 51 lb/ft3, birch 
Scrimtek achieved MOR values greater than 10,000 psi bending and MOE values of 2,3 million psi.  
Thickness swell values were slightly higher than those of aspen blocks but work in process and testing 
continues with alternative levels of added wax to control the property.  A MOE value of 2.0 million psi 
would be expected at a density of 48 lb/ft3.

6 Key Requirements for the Senneterre Project 
From a process point of view, most technical challenges have been resolved with several years of process 
improvements at the demonstration plant in Meridian.  The crush mills and scrim line have been re-
designed to improve scrim quality and consistency.  No modifications would be required on the crush 
mills and only minor changes would be desirable in the configuration of some scrim rolls.  The 
installation of a ring debarker is being considered for the plant.  Drum debarkers or Fuji Kings have been 
shown to be more efficient in removing bark from small diameter logs.  The later is widely used in OSB 
mills and is specifically installed to handle birch logs which are considered to be more difficult to debark.  
Fuji King debarkers also offer a considerable advantage in minimizing wood fibre loss when processing 
crooked logs.  More information is provided on Fuji King debarkers in Appendix I. 
 
Log conditioning is a key requirement of the ScrimtecTM process and will be an important element to 
consider in the project.  Different methods of log conditioning are used in Canadian plywood and OSB 
mills.  Spraying low pressure steam in above ground chambers is the simplest method to operate and the 
least expensive to build and maintain.  An advantage of this method is that it generates a relatively small 
amount of condensate.  Direct steam injection at higher pressure can dry the outer portion of debarked 
logs.  This problem can be mitigated by bubbling steam in a water bath or by mixing with hot water.  
Systems combing steam and water spray cost more to install and are more difficult to operate and 
maintain.  Furthermore, they generate considerably more waste water.  An alternative method is to spray 
hot water or superheated water that re-circulates through strainers.  Either method can effectively heat 
logs as long as the water flow is uniformly distributed on all wood surfaces throughout the chamber.  
High density hardwoods are most effectively conditioned in above ground vats where logs are immersed

18 of 29 

 
 

in hot water.  This is the most commonly used method of log conditioning used by Eastern Canadian OSB 
mills.  Chains are used to move logs at a steady pace.  Few of these vats are covered but most of them 
have hold-down conveyor chains to keep the logs under water.  Some will overcome the waste water 
disposal problem by re-circulating water through external heat exchangers.  The majority will have at 
least four parallel vats for log sorting by species.  
 
Total wood requirements for the plant will depend on the species used and the product mix.  Based on the 
business plan, the product mix would initially target the market for beams and headers.  Residential 
construction and light commercial buildings would be targeted for 80 percent of its production and the 
product mix would be 80 percent 2,0E and 20 percent 2,2E.  Based on pilot scale testing, Aspen 
Scrimtec™ could achieve a 2,0E at a density of 40 lb/ft3 but green loss would be expected to be around 50 
percent by volume.  Birch Scrimtec™ could achieve the same level of bending stiffness at a density of 
48 lb/ft3 but green loss including bark would be closer to 40 percent.  Furthermore, maintaining separate 
inventories of aspen and birch would increase production cost and impact productivity.  Several changes 
had to be made for each species during the course of the trial, demonstrating that process conditions 
needed to be adapted to inherent wood properties.  Mixing fibres from these two species is not 
recommended as it would inevitably lead to greater variability in product properties.  Having to deal with 
a mixed wood supply may add to the complexity of coordinating production planning with wood 
procurement.  Wood moisture content of freshly harvested birch is typically around 70 percent whereas 
aspen moisture content may be as high as 120 percent.  When dealing with small diameter pulpwood, 
there is a high probability that this would lead to greater variability in log moisture content as these 
species dry at different rates.  
 
If the log sample is representative of the wood supply available in the Senneterre area, a large proportion 
of aspen logs would need to be split.  This has been shown to impact productivity and yield.  Plant 
construction costs would also be elevated to engineer and build a green end to efficiently handle the large 
aspen logs and the small birch logs.  From process and cost point of view, it would be preferable to deal 
with birch only.  Test results have demonstrated that the full range of products can easily be produced 
from white birch.  The aspen volumes could be allocated to Norbord which operates two OSB mills in the 
Abitibi region.  The aspen logs could be traded for some of the birch logs normally processed by these 
mills.  Alternatively, small amounts of yellow birch could be mixed in if necessary.  Physical properties 
of yellow birch are similar to those of white birch and similar results would be expected from both species 
under the same process conditions.  Table 4 provides a comparison of basic properties of aspen and birch 
species.

7 Market Outlook for Scrimtec™  
A variety of engineered wood products are used in new residential construction.  These include Oriented 
Strand Lumber (OSL), Laminated Strand Lumber (LSL), Glulam, I-Joists, Laminated Veneer Lumber 
(LVL) and Parallel Strand Lumber (PSL).  OSL and LSL usually compete with solid sawnwood and are 
used for beams, headers, rimboards and structural framing lumber.  LVL and PSL have higher bending 
modulus which allows the use of longer spans and fewer pieces to carry the same loads as other 
conventional wood products.  They are also well accepted for beams and headers.  ScrimtecTM properties 
will allow for a direct substitution for LVL or PSL used in beams and headers applications (Table 5).

Both LVL and PSL provide advantages of high strength and long lengths over solid wood.  These 
advantages usually provide higher prices for these products.  Typical prices for LVL vary between $17 
and $20 per cubic foot.  Based on the properties of ScrimtecTM, it should sell a price equal or slightly 
higher than for LVL or PSL (Figure 20)  
 
Approximately 86 percent of all LVL was used in new residential construction in 2007 (Table 7).  This 
includes single family and multi family homes. Only 6 percent of the North American LVL consumption 
goes into non-residential construction and other segments. About 25 percent of LVL is used in I-beam 
flanges and 75 percent is used for beams or window and door headers.  Total North American LVL 
demand for beams and headers is expected to be 24 million cubic feet in 2009, down 33 percent from 
2008.  LVL demand is expected to increase 22 percent in 2010 and 28 percent in 2011 as the housing 
market recovers.  Based on projections from APA, the number of new housing starts is expected to 
increase by 24 percent in 2010 and 40 percent in 2011 (Table 8). 
 
Current prices for LVL are approximately $15/ft3.  Prices are expected to increase as the housing market 
recovers and demand for LVL increases.  Prices are expected to rise to approximately $20 /ft3 by 2012.

Art Schmon 
Partner, Engineered Wood Products 

•  35+ years of industry experience with engineered lumber products … most 
of that at a senior management level 

•  Co-managed the commercialization and market roll-out of Parallam® PSL in 
North America, Europe & Japan

Study Findings 

•  A substantial market opportunity exists for Scrimtec at a price level 
equivalent to 2.0E LVL 

•  The market is large enough to sustain full production from several 
Scrimtec plants 

•  Given Scrimtec’s cost advantage, the competitive geographic range will 
encompass all of North America 

•  In light of looming capacity shortages for LVL, PSL and stock glulam, 
the proposed timing of the Scrimtec start-up appears to be ideal 

•  With a cost advantage > 30% versus LVL, PSL and stock glulam, 
Scrimtec appears to be a transformative technology with a long run 
sustainable competitive advantage 

•  There appears to be minimal market risk associated with the proposed 
plant 



Background 

•  Scrimtec Industries (SI) proposes to construct a manufacturing plant in 
Val d’Or, Quebec to produce Scrimtec™, a proprietary engineered 
lumber product. 

•  FEA was asked to undertake a market study to assess the Scrimtec 
value proposition, the salability plant output capacity, likely competitive 
response and a structural composite lumber forecast from 2016 to 2030 
of supply demand costs and prices.  

•  SI requested that FEA use certain background assumptions as the 
basis for marketing study 



Key Background Assumptions Included … 
•  Plant capacity = 5.2 million ft³ 

•  Plant location: Val d’Or, Quebec 

•  All performance characteristics of Scrimtec are equal to or better than LVL or 
PSL, as produced by the major competitors 

•  MOE ≥ 2.0E – 2.2E; Fb ≥ 2900 psi; all other properties ≥ 2.0E LVL or PSL 

•  Density will range from 44 lbs/ft³ to 51 lbs/ft³ 

•  Maximum lengths will be 60’ 

•  No new or special tools will be required by builders or framers 

•  Plant start-up will be in Q4, 2017; 

•  First year of full production will be 2019, with normalized variable costs of 
$11.75/ft³

Study Conclusions 

•  A substantial market opportunity exists for Scrimtec at a price level 
equivalent to 2.0E LVL 

•  The market is large enough to sustain full production from several 
Scrimtec plants 

•  Given Scrimtec’s cost advantage, the competitive geographic range will 
encompass all of North America 

•  In light of looming capacity shortages for LVL, PSL and stock glulam, 
the proposed timing of the Scrimtec start-up appears to be ideal 

•  With a cost advantage > 30% versus LVL, PSL and stock glulam, 
Scrimtec appears to be a transformative technology with a long run 
sustainable competitive advantage 

•  There appears to be minimal market risk associated with the proposed 
plant

Study Findings 

•  A substantial market opportunity exists for Scrimtec at a price level 
equivalent to 2.0E LVL 

•  The market is large enough to sustain full production from several 
Scrimtec plants 

•  Given Scrimtec’s cost advantage, the competitive geographic range will 
encompass all of North America 

•  In light of looming capacity shortages for LVL, PSL and stock glulam, 
the proposed timing of the Scrimtec start-up appears to be ideal 

•  With a cost advantage > 30% versus LVL, PSL and stock glulam, 
Scrimtec appears to be a transformative technology with a long run 
sustainable competitive advantage 

•  There appears to be minimal market risk associated with the proposed 
plant 



Background 

•  Scrimtec Industries (SI) proposes to construct a manufacturing plant in 
Val d’Or, Quebec to produce Scrimtec™, a proprietary engineered 
lumber product. 

•  FEA was asked to undertake a market study to assess the Scrimtec 
value proposition, the salability plant output capacity, likely competitive 
response and a structural composite lumber forecast from 2016 to 2030 
of supply demand costs and prices.  

•  SI requested that FEA use certain background assumptions as the 
basis for marketing study 



Key Background Assumptions Included … 
•  Plant capacity = 5.2 million ft³ 

•  Plant location: Val d’Or, Quebec 

•  All performance characteristics of Scrimtec are equal to or better than LVL or 
PSL, as produced by the major competitors 

•  MOE ≥ 2.0E – 2.2E; Fb ≥ 2900 psi; all other properties ≥ 2.0E LVL or PSL 

•  Density will range from 44 lbs/ft³ to 51 lbs/ft³ 

•  Maximum lengths will be 60’ 

•  No new or special tools will be required by builders or framers 

•  Plant start-up will be in Q4, 2017; 

•  First year of full production will be 2019, with normalized variable costs of 
$11.75/ft³

Business Models & Market Strategies 

Boise Cascade 

§  # 1 in the N.A. market and the most formidable competitor

builders … margin squeeze! 

§  Major shareholder, Dearborn Madison, has excited the business; 
capacity expansion is likely

Weyerhaeuser 

§  # 2 in the N.A. market with the broadest range of ELPs, including PSL 
and LSL (the remains of Trus Joist Corp) 

§  Has rationalized its product lines to minimize cannibalization 

§  Coast-to-coast 2-step distribution through its own 21 distributors and

Study Conclusions 

•  A substantial market opportunity exists for Scrimtec at a price level 
equivalent to 2.0E LVL 

•  The market is large enough to sustain full production from several 
Scrimtec plants 

•  Given Scrimtec’s cost advantage, the competitive geographic range will 
encompass all of North America 

•  In light of looming capacity shortages for LVL, PSL and stock glulam, 
the proposed timing of the Scrimtec start-up appears to be ideal 

•  With a cost advantage > 30% versus LVL, PSL and stock glulam, 
Scrimtec appears to be a transformative technology with a long run 
sustainable competitive advantage 

•  There appears to be minimal market risk associated with the proposed 
plant

Art Schmon 
Partner, Engineered Wood Products 

•  35+ years of industry experience with engineered lumber products … most 
of that at a senior management level 

•  Co-managed the commercialization and market roll-out of Parallam® PSL in 
North America, Europe & Japan 

•  Managed the start-up of Trus Joist MacMillan's European and Middle East

•  Managed the Introduction of I-joists, PSL and LSL into the European Market 

•  BA, Princeton University;  MBA Simon Fraser University 



Study Findings 

•  A substantial market opportunity exists for Scrimtec at a price level 
equivalent to 2.0E LVL 

•  The market is large enough to sustain full production from several 
Scrimtec plants 

•  Given Scrimtec’s cost advantage, the competitive geographic range will 
encompass all of North America 

•  In light of looming capacity shortages for LVL, PSL and stock glulam, 
the proposed timing of the Scrimtec start-up appears to be ideal 

•  With a cost advantage > 30% versus LVL, PSL and stock glulam, 
Scrimtec appears to be a transformative technology with a long run 
sustainable competitive advantage 

•  There appears to be minimal market risk associated with the proposed 
plant 



Background 

•  Scrimtec Industries (SI) proposes to construct a manufacturing plant in 
Val d’Or, Quebec to produce Scrimtec™, a proprietary engineered 
lumber product. 

•  FEA was asked to undertake a market study to assess the Scrimtec 
value proposition, the salability plant output capacity, likely competitive 
response and a structural composite lumber forecast from 2016 to 2030 
of supply demand costs and prices.  

•  SI requested that FEA use certain background assumptions as the 
basis for marketing study 



Key Background Assumptions Included … 
•  Plant capacity = 5.2 million ft³ 

•  Plant location: Val d’Or, Quebec 

•  All performance characteristics of Scrimtec are equal to or better than LVL or 
PSL, as produced by the major competitors 

•  MOE ≥ 2.0E – 2.2E; Fb ≥ 2900 psi; all other properties ≥ 2.0E LVL or PSL 

•  Density will range from 44 lbs/ft³ to 51 lbs/ft³ 

•  Maximum lengths will be 60’ 

•  No new or special tools will be required by builders or framers 

•  Plant start-up will be in Q4, 2017; 

•  First year of full production will be 2019, with normalized variable costs of 
$11.75/ft³

Scrimtec Competition 
Business Models & Market Strategies 

Boise Cascade 

§  # 1 in the N.A. market and the most formidable competitor 

§  Market engineered framing systems composed of LVL, Glulam, I-Joists, 
Connectors, hangers, software, engineering/technical support and a 
life-of-structure warrantee 

§  Coast-to-coast 2-step distribution through 60 yards, 31 wholly owned 
and 30 independent 

§  Company offers discounts to pro-dealers and rebates to large builders 

§  In order to grow market share, Boise is pursuing the big national 
builders … margin squeeze! 

§  Major shareholder, Dearborn Madison, has excited the business; 
capacity expansion is likely 



Scrimtec Competition 
Business Models & Market Strategies 

Weyerhaeuser 

§  # 2 in the N.A. market with the broadest range of ELPs, including PSL 
and LSL (the remains of Trus Joist Corp) 

§  Has rationalized its product lines to minimize cannibalization 

§  Coast-to-coast 2-step distribution through its own 21 distributors and 
several independent yards 

§  Also pursues the big builders with aggressive rebate programs 

§  Has lost half of its market share over the past 15 years 

§  Took the biggest capacity hit during the recession 

§  Recently embarked on a 4-year program in Eugene to replace eight 2-
foot presses with five 4-foot presses which will add ≈ 1.2 MM Ft³ 

§  New management; draconian cost cuts; better performance; new

Louisiana Pacific 

§  # 3 in the N.A. market

§  Is betting the farm on LSL as a substitute for LVL … bad bet in our view 

§  Coast-to-coast 2-step distribution through independent yards

§  # 4 in sales but likely #1 in terms of unit volume profit

1 Background 
Scrimtec™ is an engineered wood product manufactured from small-diameter trees.  The technology was 
initially conceived in Australia by the Commonwealth Scientific Industrial Research Organization and the 
rights were acquired by TimTek in 2002.  A screening of research universities was conducted to 
determine where to further develop the technology and Mississippi State University was selected to 
demonstrate that the newly patented press would work with many species.  Shuqualak Lumber Co. 
licensed the production rights in the tree growing area east of the continental divide in North America in 
2005 and assembled a demonstration plant in Meridian Mississippi in 2006 where industrial production 
techniques have been optimized and demonstrated through years of research. 
 
Initial results on pine plantation thinnings indicate that Scrimtec™ has the potential to compete 
favourably with beams and timbers used in residential and commercial construction.  Shuqualak Lumber 
Co. has a license agreement to build a plant and is currently evaluating a project in Senneterre.  The wood 
supply available for the plant would be made up of trembling aspen and white birch.  No data was 
available to date on the properties of Scrimtec™ products made from these species.  A full truck load of 
aspen and birch logs was shipped to Meridian in August 2009 to evaluate the suitability of these species 
for this process.  
 
 

2 Objectives 
The general objectives of this project are: 
 

• Review recent process developments in Scrimtec™ technology 
• Identify specific process conditions for aspen & birch 
• Evaluate the suitability of aspen & birch pulpwood grade in terms of process efficiency and 

product quality 
• Identify key requirements for a manufacturing facility to be located in Senneterre 

 
 

3 Staff 
Gilles Brunette Manager Composite Wood Products-Forintek division 
François Robichaud Research Scientist, Forest Products Marketing-FPInnovations Forintek 
Patrick Lavoie  Research Scientist, Forest Products Marketing-FPInnovations Forintek

2 of 29 

 
 

 

4 Process Description 
4.1 Log Preparation 
This part of the process is very similar to the green end of oriented strand board plants (OSB).  Tree 
lengths are slashed into 10-foot lengths and debarked.  Logs larger than 8-inch diameter are split into 
smaller blocks.  The blocks are scored and conditioned in steam heated vats to core temperature of 100-
1400F (38-600C). 
 
4.2 Scrimming & Mat Preparation 
Individual blocks are fed through a series of crushing rolls.  Five sets of crushing rolls are used to prepare 
the material for the scrim line.  A significant amount of free water is removed during this process. 
 
 

 
Figure 1 Side view of crush mills 
 
The outfeed from the crush mills feeds into the scrim line.  Seven sets of scrim rolls are used to 
progressively break up the blocks into long fibre mats.  Each set of scrim rolls is designed differently to 
minimize fibre damage and achieve the appropriate strand length.  The scrim line is designed with a 6-
inch gap between each transfer belt leading to the next set of rolls.  This ensures that the fines and 
residual bark are removed from the mats.

3 of 29 

 
 

 
 

 
Figure 2 Block in transition from crush mill outfeed to scrim mill infeed

4 of 29

5 of 29 

 
 

Each mat is scarfed on both ends, weighed and scanned to determine mat volume and a resulting initial 
mat density is calculated.  Operating parameters are then calculated and each mat is densified to a 
constant bulk density to optimize production in the plant.  Densified mats are combined into a continuous 
layer and trimmed to a standard length and width. 
 
 

 
Figure 4 Fibre mats exiting the scrim line 
 
4.3 Drying and Resination 
Fibres are dried in a conveyor dryer at 3200F (1600C) to a target moisture content of 8 percent.  An 
exterior-grade adhesive is applied by spray.  A diluted solution of phenol-formaldehyde adhesive is used 
to ensure full coverage and penetration into the wood.  A second stage of drying is used to achieve a final 
moisture content of about 8 percent.  Figure 5 illustrates the drying and resination process.

Confidential 
 
 

 

 

© 2009 FPInnovations – Forintek Division. All rights reserved. 
 

6 of 29 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Figure 5 Schematic representation of the drying and resin application process 
 
 
4.4 Mat Lay-Up & Pressing 
The continuous fibre mat exiting the final dryer is ripped into 3-4-foot wide strips.  The individual strips 
are then laid in multiple layers in a card deck fashion with a 1-foot overlap to form a continuous billet.  A 
flying cut-off saw cuts the block into 49-foot billets.  
 

 
Figure 6 Fibre mat ready for pressing

The billets are individually hot pressed to final thicknesses ranging from 1¾-inch to 7 inches.  The press 
is designed with an internal rectangular pressure vessel and hydraulic cylinders on the X and Y axes.  
Steam injection in combination with the pressure vessel technology is used to achieve full curing of the 
phenol formaldehyde adhesive in a relatively short period of time.  A 3-inch thick billet may be pressed in 
approximately 11 minutes.  Unlike conventional hot pressing, heat conductivity with steam injection and 
pressure vessel technology is not significantly impacted by panel thickness. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
Figure 7 Schematic view of the press 
 
 
4.1 Product Finishing 
The billets are hot stacked and conditioned for 24 hours. Each billet will be scanned by X-Ray to map out 
horizontal density variations.  The billets are cut to size, sanded, coated with wax.  Products are 
individually wrapped and ready to be loaded and shipped.

5 Pilot Scale Tests with Aspen & Birch 
5.1 Material Preparation 
A representative sample of aspen and birch logs was collected from the Senneterre region and shipped to 
Meridian, Mississippi in August 2009.  The truck arrived in Meridian on August 24 with 33,924 lb of 
Aspen and Birch blocks.  There were 52 Aspen logs weighing 17,010 lb and 230 Birch logs weighing 
16,914 lb.  The general specifications for the logs selected were as follows: 
 

• 3" minimum small end diameter 
• 8'' maximum large end diameter 
• Cut to 96" length 
• Full bark on 
• No tops from larger diameter trees such as sawlogs 
• No rot, dry, dead, forks, splits, burned or excessive crook blocks 
• No excessive swelled butts (should not exceed 1/4 of the butt diameter) 
• Birch and Aspen were segregated and tied into bundles prior to shipment

The expected outcome of these tests included: 
 

• Demonstration that aspen or birch could be used to produce Scrimtec™ with strength properties 
equivalent or better than those of products made from pine   

• Determine if the aspen and birch will break down adequately using the Scrimming process 
• Determine minimum requirements in order to achieve desired results 

♦ Required density 
♦ Required resin loading and dilution factor 
♦ Dryer throughput rate 
♦ Press time 
♦ Wood recovery 

• Using the process variables from above determine the impact to the cost structure 
 
 
Each bundle was unloaded from the truck, weighed and tagged.  There were 9 bundles of Birch and 
8 bundles of Aspen.  Each bundle of Birch was opened and every log was measured, weighed and tagged 
with a unique number.  Moisture content samples were obtained from each bundle.  The logs were moved 
into a pit still strapped together in bundles.  After all the bundles were in the pit, it was filled with water 
to preserve the blocks during the testing period.  
 

 
Figure 9 Log storage during testing period 
 
Some blocks were cut into 6 pieces in order to make them small enough to convey to the crush mills and 
down the scrim line.  Block diameter is limited based on the width of the scrim line to meet initial density

6 Key Requirements for the Senneterre Project 
From a process point of view, most technical challenges have been resolved with several years of process 
improvements at the demonstration plant in Meridian.  The crush mills and scrim line have been re-
designed to improve scrim quality and consistency.  No modifications would be required on the crush 
mills and only minor changes would be desirable in the configuration of some scrim rolls.  The 
installation of a ring debarker is being considered for the plant.  Drum debarkers or Fuji Kings have been 
shown to be more efficient in removing bark from small diameter logs.  The later is widely used in OSB 
mills and is specifically installed to handle birch logs which are considered to be more difficult to debark.  
Fuji King debarkers also offer a considerable advantage in minimizing wood fibre loss when processing 
crooked logs.  More information is provided on Fuji King debarkers in Appendix I. 
 
Log conditioning is a key requirement of the ScrimtecTM process and will be an important element to 
consider in the project.  Different methods of log conditioning are used in Canadian plywood and OSB 
mills.  Spraying low pressure steam in above ground chambers is the simplest method to operate and the 
least expensive to build and maintain.  An advantage of this method is that it generates a relatively small 
amount of condensate.  Direct steam injection at higher pressure can dry the outer portion of debarked 
logs.  This problem can be mitigated by bubbling steam in a water bath or by mixing with hot water.  
Systems combing steam and water spray cost more to install and are more difficult to operate and 
maintain.  Furthermore, they generate considerably more waste water.  An alternative method is to spray 
hot water or superheated water that re-circulates through strainers.  Either method can effectively heat 
logs as long as the water flow is uniformly distributed on all wood surfaces throughout the chamber.  
High density hardwoods are most effectively conditioned in above ground vats where logs are immersed

mills.  Chains are used to move logs at a steady pace.  Few of these vats are covered but most of them 
have hold-down conveyor chains to keep the logs under water.  Some will overcome the waste water 
disposal problem by re-circulating water through external heat exchangers.  The majority will have at 
least four parallel vats for log sorting by species.  
 
Total wood requirements for the plant will depend on the species used and the product mix.  Based on the 
business plan, the product mix would initially target the market for beams and headers.  Residential 
construction and light commercial buildings would be targeted for 80 percent of its production and the 
product mix would be 80 percent 2,0E and 20 percent 2,2E.  Based on pilot scale testing, Aspen 
Scrimtec™ could achieve a 2,0E at a density of 40 lb/ft3 but green loss would be expected to be around 50 
percent by volume.  Birch Scrimtec™ could achieve the same level of bending stiffness at a density of 
48 lb/ft3 but green loss including bark would be closer to 40 percent.  Furthermore, maintaining separate 
inventories of aspen and birch would increase production cost and impact productivity.  Several changes 
had to be made for each species during the course of the trial, demonstrating that process conditions 
needed to be adapted to inherent wood properties.  Mixing fibres from these two species is not 
recommended as it would inevitably lead to greater variability in product properties.  Having to deal with 
a mixed wood supply may add to the complexity of coordinating production planning with wood 
procurement.  Wood moisture content of freshly harvested birch is typically around 70 percent whereas 
aspen moisture content may be as high as 120 percent.  When dealing with small diameter pulpwood, 
there is a high probability that this would lead to greater variability in log moisture content as these 
species dry at different rates.  
 
If the log sample is representative of the wood supply available in the Senneterre area, a large proportion 
of aspen logs would need to be split.  This has been shown to impact productivity and yield.  Plant 
construction costs would also be elevated to engineer and build a green end to efficiently handle the large 
aspen logs and the small birch logs.  From process and cost point of view, it would be preferable to deal 
with birch only.  Test results have demonstrated that the full range of products can easily be produced 
from white birch.  The aspen volumes could be allocated to Norbord which operates two OSB mills in the 
Abitibi region.  The aspen logs could be traded for some of the birch logs normally processed by these 
mills.  Alternatively, small amounts of yellow birch could be mixed in if necessary.  Physical properties 
of yellow birch are similar to those of white birch and similar results would be expected from both species

7 Market Outlook for Scrimtec™  
A variety of engineered wood products are used in new residential construction.  These include Oriented 
Strand Lumber (OSL), Laminated Strand Lumber (LSL), Glulam, I-Joists, Laminated Veneer Lumber 
(LVL) and Parallel Strand Lumber (PSL).  OSL and LSL usually compete with solid sawnwood and are 
used for beams, headers, rimboards and structural framing lumber.  LVL and PSL have higher bending 
modulus which allows the use of longer spans and fewer pieces to carry the same loads as other 
conventional wood products.  They are also well accepted for beams and headers.  ScrimtecTM properties 
will allow for a direct substitution for LVL or PSL used in beams and headers applications (Table 5).

advantages usually provide higher prices for these products.  Typical prices for LVL vary between $17 
and $20 per cubic foot.  Based on the properties of ScrimtecTM, it should sell a price equal or slightly 
higher than for LVL or PSL (Figure 20)  
 
Approximately 86 percent of all LVL was used in new residential construction in 2007 (Table 7).  This 
includes single family and multi family homes. Only 6 percent of the North American LVL consumption 
goes into non-residential construction and other segments. About 25 percent of LVL is used in I-beam 
flanges and 75 percent is used for beams or window and door headers.  Total North American LVL 
demand for beams and headers is expected to be 24 million cubic feet in 2009, down 33 percent from 
2008.  LVL demand is expected to increase 22 percent in 2010 and 28 percent in 2011 as the housing 
market recovers.  Based on projections from APA, the number of new housing starts is expected to 
increase by 24 percent in 2010 and 40 percent in 2011 (Table 8). 
 
Current prices for LVL are approximately $15/ft3.  Prices are expected to increase as the housing market 
recovers and demand for LVL increases.  Prices are expected to rise to approximately $20 /ft3 by 2012.

1 Background 
Scrimtec™ is an engineered wood product manufactured from small-diameter trees.  The technology was 
initially conceived in Australia by the Commonwealth Scientific Industrial Research Organization and the 
rights were acquired by TimTek in 2002.  A screening of research universities was conducted to 
determine where to further develop the technology and Mississippi State University was selected to 
demonstrate that the newly patented press would work with many species.  Shuqualak Lumber Co. 
licensed the production rights in the tree growing area east of the continental divide in North America in 
2005 and assembled a demonstration plant in Meridian Mississippi in 2006 where industrial production 
techniques have been optimized and demonstrated through years of research. 
 
Initial results on pine plantation thinnings indicate that Scrimtec™ has the potential to compete 
favourably with beams and timbers used in residential and commercial construction.  Shuqualak Lumber 
Co. has a license agreement to build a plant and is currently evaluating a project in Senneterre.  The wood 
supply available for the plant would be made up of trembling aspen and white birch.  No data was 
available to date on the properties of Scrimtec™ products made from these species.  A full truck load of 
aspen and birch logs was shipped to Meridian in August 2009 to evaluate the suitability of these species 
for this process.  
 
 

2 Objectives 
The general objectives of this project are: 
 

• Review recent process developments in Scrimtec™ technology 
• Identify specific process conditions for aspen & birch 
• Evaluate the suitability of aspen & birch pulpwood grade in terms of process efficiency and 

product quality 
• Identify key requirements for a manufacturing facility to be located in Senneterre 

 
 

3 Staff

François Robichaud Research Scientist, Forest Products Marketing-FPInnovations Forintek 
Patrick Lavoie  Research Scientist, Forest Products Marketing-FPInnovations Forintek

4 Process Description 
4.1 Log Preparation 
This part of the process is very similar to the green end of oriented strand board plants (OSB).  Tree 
lengths are slashed into 10-foot lengths and debarked.  Logs larger than 8-inch diameter are split into 
smaller blocks.  The blocks are scored and conditioned in steam heated vats to core temperature of 100-
1400F (38-600C). 
 
4.2 Scrimming & Mat Preparation 
Individual blocks are fed through a series of crushing rolls.  Five sets of crushing rolls are used to prepare 
the material for the scrim line.  A significant amount of free water is removed during this process. 
 
 

 
Figure 1 Side view of crush mills 
 
The outfeed from the crush mills feeds into the scrim line.  Seven sets of scrim rolls are used to 
progressively break up the blocks into long fibre mats.  Each set of scrim rolls is designed differently to 
minimize fibre damage and achieve the appropriate strand length.  The scrim line is designed with a 6-
inch gap between each transfer belt leading to the next set of rolls.  This ensures that the fines and 
residual bark are removed from the mats.

6 Key Requirements for the Senneterre Project 
From a process point of view, most technical challenges have been resolved with several years of process 
improvements at the demonstration plant in Meridian.  The crush mills and scrim line have been re-
designed to improve scrim quality and consistency.  No modifications would be required on the crush 
mills and only minor changes would be desirable in the configuration of some scrim rolls.  The 
installation of a ring debarker is being considered for the plant.  Drum debarkers or Fuji Kings have been 
shown to be more efficient in removing bark from small diameter logs.  The later is widely used in OSB 
mills and is specifically installed to handle birch logs which are considered to be more difficult to debark.  
Fuji King debarkers also offer a considerable advantage in minimizing wood fibre loss when processing 
crooked logs.  More information is provided on Fuji King debarkers in Appendix I. 
 
Log conditioning is a key requirement of the ScrimtecTM process and will be an important element to 
consider in the project.  Different methods of log conditioning are used in Canadian plywood and OSB 
mills.  Spraying low pressure steam in above ground chambers is the simplest method to operate and the 
least expensive to build and maintain.  An advantage of this method is that it generates a relatively small 
amount of condensate.  Direct steam injection at higher pressure can dry the outer portion of debarked 
logs.  This problem can be mitigated by bubbling steam in a water bath or by mixing with hot water.  
Systems combing steam and water spray cost more to install and are more difficult to operate and 
maintain.  Furthermore, they generate considerably more waste water.  An alternative method is to spray 
hot water or superheated water that re-circulates through strainers.  Either method can effectively heat 
logs as long as the water flow is uniformly distributed on all wood surfaces throughout the chamber.  
High density hardwoods are most effectively conditioned in above ground vats where logs are immersed

in hot water.  This is the most commonly used method of log conditioning used by Eastern Canadian OSB 
mills.  Chains are used to move logs at a steady pace.  Few of these vats are covered but most of them 
have hold-down conveyor chains to keep the logs under water.  Some will overcome the waste water 
disposal problem by re-circulating water through external heat exchangers.  The majority will have at 
least four parallel vats for log sorting by species.  
 
Total wood requirements for the plant will depend on the species used and the product mix.  Based on the 
business plan, the product mix would initially target the market for beams and headers.  Residential 
construction and light commercial buildings would be targeted for 80 percent of its production and the 
product mix would be 80 percent 2,0E and 20 percent 2,2E.  Based on pilot scale testing, Aspen 
Scrimtec™ could achieve a 2,0E at a density of 40 lb/ft3 but green loss would be expected to be around 50 
percent by volume.  Birch Scrimtec™ could achieve the same level of bending stiffness at a density of 
48 lb/ft3 but green loss including bark would be closer to 40 percent.  Furthermore, maintaining separate 
inventories of aspen and birch would increase production cost and impact productivity.  Several changes 
had to be made for each species during the course of the trial, demonstrating that process conditions 
needed to be adapted to inherent wood properties.  Mixing fibres from these two species is not 
recommended as it would inevitably lead to greater variability in product properties.  Having to deal with 
a mixed wood supply may add to the complexity of coordinating production planning with wood 
procurement.  Wood moisture content of freshly harvested birch is typically around 70 percent whereas 
aspen moisture content may be as high as 120 percent.  When dealing with small diameter pulpwood, 
there is a high probability that this would lead to greater variability in log moisture content as these 
species dry at different rates.  
 
If the log sample is representative of the wood supply available in the Senneterre area, a large proportion 
of aspen logs would need to be split.  This has been shown to impact productivity and yield.  Plant 
construction costs would also be elevated to engineer and build a green end to efficiently handle the large 
aspen logs and the small birch logs.  From process and cost point of view, it would be preferable to deal 
with birch only.  Test results have demonstrated that the full range of products can easily be produced 
from white birch.  The aspen volumes could be allocated to Norbord which operates two OSB mills in the 
Abitibi region.  The aspen logs could be traded for some of the birch logs normally processed by these 
mills.  Alternatively, small amounts of yellow birch could be mixed in if necessary.  Physical properties 
of yellow birch are similar to those of white birch and similar results would be expected from both species 
under the same process conditions.  Table 4 provides a comparison of basic properties of aspen and birch 
species.

7 Market Outlook for Scrimtec™  
A variety of engineered wood products are used in new residential construction.  These include Oriented 
Strand Lumber (OSL), Laminated Strand Lumber (LSL), Glulam, I-Joists, Laminated Veneer Lumber 
(LVL) and Parallel Strand Lumber (PSL).  OSL and LSL usually compete with solid sawnwood and are 
used for beams, headers, rimboards and structural framing lumber.  LVL and PSL have higher bending 
modulus which allows the use of longer spans and fewer pieces to carry the same loads as other 
conventional wood products.  They are also well accepted for beams and headers.  ScrimtecTM properties 
will allow for a direct substitution for LVL or PSL used in beams and headers applications (Table 5).

Both LVL and PSL provide advantages of high strength and long lengths over solid wood.  These 
advantages usually provide higher prices for these products.  Typical prices for LVL vary between $17 
and $20 per cubic foot.  Based on the properties of ScrimtecTM, it should sell a price equal or slightly 
higher than for LVL or PSL (Figure 20)  
 
Approximately 86 percent of all LVL was used in new residential construction in 2007 (Table 7).  This 
includes single family and multi family homes. Only 6 percent of the North American LVL consumption 
goes into non-residential construction and other segments. About 25 percent of LVL is used in I-beam 
flanges and 75 percent is used for beams or window and door headers.  Total North American LVL 
demand for beams and headers is expected to be 24 million cubic feet in 2009, down 33 percent from 
2008.  LVL demand is expected to increase 22 percent in 2010 and 28 percent in 2011 as the housing 
market recovers.  Based on projections from APA, the number of new housing starts is expected to 
increase by 24 percent in 2010 and 40 percent in 2011 (Table 8). 
 
Current prices for LVL are approximately $15/ft3.  Prices are expected to increase as the housing market 
recovers and demand for LVL increases.  Prices are expected to rise to approximately $20 /ft3 by 2012.

1 Background 
Scrimtec™ is an engineered wood product manufactured from small-diameter trees.  The technology was 
initially conceived in Australia by the Commonwealth Scientific Industrial Research Organization and the 
rights were acquired by TimTek in 2002.  A screening of research universities was conducted to 
determine where to further develop the technology and Mississippi State University was selected to 
demonstrate that the newly patented press would work with many species.  Shuqualak Lumber Co. 
licensed the production rights in the tree growing area east of the continental divide in North America in 
2005 and assembled a demonstration plant in Meridian Mississippi in 2006 where industrial production 
techniques have been optimized and demonstrated through years of research. 
 
Initial results on pine plantation thinnings indicate that Scrimtec™ has the potential to compete 
favourably with beams and timbers used in residential and commercial construction.  Shuqualak Lumber 
Co. has a license agreement to build a plant and is currently evaluating a project in Senneterre.  The wood 
supply available for the plant would be made up of trembling aspen and white birch.  No data was 
available to date on the properties of Scrimtec™ products made from these species.  A full truck load of 
aspen and birch logs was shipped to Meridian in August 2009 to evaluate the suitability of these species 
for this process.  
 
 

2 Objectives 
The general objectives of this project are: 
 

• Review recent process developments in Scrimtec™ technology 
• Identify specific process conditions for aspen & birch 
• Evaluate the suitability of aspen & birch pulpwood grade in terms of process efficiency and 

product quality 
• Identify key requirements for a manufacturing facility to be located in Senneterre

4 Process Description 
4.1 Log Preparation 
This part of the process is very similar to the green end of oriented strand board plants (OSB).  Tree 
lengths are slashed into 10-foot lengths and debarked.  Logs larger than 8-inch diameter are split into 
smaller blocks.  The blocks are scored and conditioned in steam heated vats to core temperature of 100-
1400F (38-600C). 
 
4.2 Scrimming & Mat Preparation 
Individual blocks are fed through a series of crushing rolls.  Five sets of crushing rolls are used to prepare 
the material for the scrim line.  A significant amount of free water is removed during this process. 
 
 

 
Figure 1 Side view of crush mills 
 
The outfeed from the crush mills feeds into the scrim line.  Seven sets of scrim rolls are used to 
progressively break up the blocks into long fibre mats.  Each set of scrim rolls is designed differently to 
minimize fibre damage and achieve the appropriate strand length.  The scrim line is designed with a 6-
inch gap between each transfer belt leading to the next set of rolls.  This ensures that the fines and 
residual bark are removed from the mats.

Each mat is scarfed on both ends, weighed and scanned to determine mat volume and a resulting initial

4.3 Drying and Resination 
Fibres are dried in a conveyor dryer at 3200F (1600C) to a target moisture content of 8 percent.  An 
exterior-grade adhesive is applied by spray.  A diluted solution of phenol-formaldehyde adhesive is used 
to ensure full coverage and penetration into the wood.  A second stage of drying is used to achieve a final 
moisture content of about 8 percent.  Figure 5 illustrates the drying and resination process.

5.1 Test Results & Observations 
5.1.1 Material recovery 
Total green end loss (before drying) was estimated at 51% for aspen on a volume basis and 42% for birch.  
Bark volume was slightly larger for aspen logs but the difference is explained mainly by the splitting loss.  
Blocks split by sawing tended to break up in the scrimming process due to cut grain, while blocks split with 
wedges produced long fibre mats.  Aspen fibre losses were higher due to multiple splits and damaging pieces 
during the wedge splitting process.  Details on material loss at each stage of the process are provided in 
Table 1.  The cut-to-length losses reported in Table 1 are calculated based on projected deliveries of tree-
length logs to the production facility.  Additionally, 7% of the reported loss is free water being squeezed out of 
each block during the scrimming process which is advantageous in equalizing the moisture content for 
densifying calculations and drying processes.

6 Key Requirements for the Senneterre Project 
From a process point of view, most technical challenges have been resolved with several years of process 
improvements at the demonstration plant in Meridian.  The crush mills and scrim line have been re-
designed to improve scrim quality and consistency.  No modifications would be required on the crush 
mills and only minor changes would be desirable in the configuration of some scrim rolls.  The 
installation of a ring debarker is being considered for the plant.  Drum debarkers or Fuji Kings have been 
shown to be more efficient in removing bark from small diameter logs.  The later is widely used in OSB 
mills and is specifically installed to handle birch logs which are considered to be more difficult to debark.  
Fuji King debarkers also offer a considerable advantage in minimizing wood fibre loss when processing 
crooked logs.  More information is provided on Fuji King debarkers in Appendix I. 
 
Log conditioning is a key requirement of the ScrimtecTM process and will be an important element to 
consider in the project.  Different methods of log conditioning are used in Canadian plywood and OSB 
mills.  Spraying low pressure steam in above ground chambers is the simplest method to operate and the 
least expensive to build and maintain.  An advantage of this method is that it generates a relatively small 
amount of condensate.  Direct steam injection at higher pressure can dry the outer portion of debarked 
logs.  This problem can be mitigated by bubbling steam in a water bath or by mixing with hot water.  
Systems combing steam and water spray cost more to install and are more difficult to operate and 
maintain.  Furthermore, they generate considerably more waste water.  An alternative method is to spray 
hot water or superheated water that re-circulates through strainers.  Either method can effectively heat 
logs as long as the water flow is uniformly distributed on all wood surfaces throughout the chamber.  
High density hardwoods are most effectively conditioned in above ground vats where logs are immersed

Total wood requirements for the plant will depend on the species used and the product mix.  Based on the 
business plan, the product mix would initially target the market for beams and headers.  Residential 
construction and light commercial buildings would be targeted for 80 percent of its production and the 
product mix would be 80 percent 2,0E and 20 percent 2,2E.  Based on pilot scale testing, Aspen 
Scrimtec™ could achieve a 2,0E at a density of 40 lb/ft3 but green loss would be expected to be around 50 
percent by volume.  Birch Scrimtec™ could achieve the same level of bending stiffness at a density of 
48 lb/ft3 but green loss including bark would be closer to 40 percent.  Furthermore, maintaining separate 
inventories of aspen and birch would increase production cost and impact productivity.  Several changes 
had to be made for each species during the course of the trial, demonstrating that process conditions 
needed to be adapted to inherent wood properties.  Mixing fibres from these two species is not 
recommended as it would inevitably lead to greater variability in product properties.  Having to deal with 
a mixed wood supply may add to the complexity of coordinating production planning with wood 
procurement.  Wood moisture content of freshly harvested birch is typically around 70 percent whereas 
aspen moisture content may be as high as 120 percent.  When dealing with small diameter pulpwood, 
there is a high probability that this would lead to greater variability in log moisture content as these 
species dry at different rates.  
 
If the log sample is representative of the wood supply available in the Senneterre area, a large proportion 
of aspen logs would need to be split.  This has been shown to impact productivity and yield.  Plant 
construction costs would also be elevated to engineer and build a green end to efficiently handle the large 
aspen logs and the small birch logs.  From process and cost point of view, it would be preferable to deal 
with birch only.  Test results have demonstrated that the full range of products can easily be produced 
from white birch.  The aspen volumes could be allocated to Norbord which operates two OSB mills in the 
Abitibi region.  The aspen logs could be traded for some of the birch logs normally processed by these 
mills.  Alternatively, small amounts of yellow birch could be mixed in if necessary.  Physical properties 
of yellow birch are similar to those of white birch and similar results would be expected from both species

7 Market Outlook for Scrimtec™  
A variety of engineered wood products are used in new residential construction.  These include Oriented 
Strand Lumber (OSL), Laminated Strand Lumber (LSL), Glulam, I-Joists, Laminated Veneer Lumber 
(LVL) and Parallel Strand Lumber (PSL).  OSL and LSL usually compete with solid sawnwood and are 
used for beams, headers, rimboards and structural framing lumber.  LVL and PSL have higher bending 
modulus which allows the use of longer spans and fewer pieces to carry the same loads as other 
conventional wood products.  They are also well accepted for beams and headers.  ScrimtecTM properties 
will allow for a direct substitution for LVL or PSL used in beams and headers applications (Table 5).

Laminated Veneer Lumber (LVL) is an engineered wood product that is made by bonding thin wood veneers together under heat and pressure. The veneers are typically oriented in the same direction to enhance the product's strength and stiffness. LVL is used primarily as structural framing for residential and commercial construction, including beams, headers, rafters, and columns. Its uniformity and ability to bear heavy loads over wide spans make it a popular choice for areas requiring high structural integrity.
The current market for Laminated Veneer Lumber (LVL) is experiencing positive growth, driven by its increasing adoption in construction due to its strength, durability, and environmental benefits. The global LVL market was valued at approximately USD 5.4 billion in 2023 and is projected to grow to USD 6.7 billion by 2032, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of around 2.5% during this period (Research & Markets).
The demand for LVL is particularly strong in the construction sector, where it's used for beams, headers, and other structural components. This demand is bolstered by LVL's attributes such as high strength, uniformity, and its ability to be used in various applications including residential, commercial, and industrial construction (Expert Market Research).
Additionally, the market growth is supported by a shift towards sustainable construction materials. LVL is favored for its environmental advantages, being made from renewable wood resources, and its manufacturing process is considered to be more eco-friendly compared to traditional construction materials like steel and concrete (Dataintelo) (Credence Research).
Key players in the market are focusing on competitive pricing, quality improvement, and expanding their market reach through strategic partnerships and technological advancements in manufacturing processes (Dataintelo).
Overall, the LVL market is set to continue its growth trajectory, driven by both increasing environmental awareness and the material's inherent structural benefits.
Currently, the supply of Laminated Veneer Lumber (LVL) generally meets the market demand, although there are challenges. The market for LVL is growing, with increases in both supply capacity and consumption. For instance, in North America, the market size is expected to grow from 2.2 million cubic meters in 2022 to an estimated 2.4 million cubic meters by 2028, indicating a steady growth in supply alongside demand (GlobeNewswire).
However, there are some challenges affecting the balance of supply and demand. Price fluctuations of raw materials, especially high-quality wood veneers, can impact production costs and profitability for LVL manufacturers. This could potentially affect supply levels if costs become too prohibitive (Credence Research). Additionally, the bulky and heavy nature of LVL presents transportation challenges, which can limit the geographic reach of some producers, affecting their ability to meet regional demands efficiently (Credence Research).
Despite these challenges, the overall market dynamics suggest that the supply of LVL is keeping pace with the demand, supported by strategic expansions and technological advancements in production processes (IMARC).

   - **Construction Industry Cycles:** The demand for LVL is closely tied to the construction industry, which is subject to economic cycles. A downturn in construction activity could reduce demand for LVL products.
   - **Interest Rates and Financing Costs:** Changes in interest rates can affect the cost of financing the new plant, potentially impacting profitability.

3. **Competitive Landscape:**
   - **New Entrants:** The entry of new competitors with similar or superior technologies could erode market share and affect pricing power.
   - **Technological Advancements:** Rapid advancements in alternative construction materials or processes could make LVL less competitive.

4. **Regulatory and Environmental Risks:**
   - **Regulatory Changes:** Changes in building codes, environmental regulations, or trade policies could impact production processes and market access.
   - **Sustainability Standards:** Increasing emphasis on sustainability may require additional investments in eco-friendly practices and certifications, impacting costs.

5. **Market Acceptance:**

6. **Global Trade Dynamics:**

   - **Scalability:** Scaling up production from a pilot plant to full-scale commercial operation may present unforeseen challenges and inefficiencies.

metadata.text:
> 
> "In one of the most thrilling finales in the history of the Olympic regattas, the thin cedar prow of the unbeaten and unbeatable Husky Clipper edged across the line of the Langersee [sic] a mere deck's length ahead of Italy with Germany a corresponding distance behind in third place" ("Fifth Successive Olympic Eight-Oared …").

The Seattle Times used the copy of Paul Mickelson, an Associated Press sportswriter:

> "Kick … The gallant Washington eight-oared crew will go down in the record books as the mightiest of them all. The Huskies, with a finishing 'kick' that made history, swept everything in sight to earn their fame.
> 
> "They should be called the 'Finishers" instead of the Huskies" ("Never to Forget …").

What Makes a Legend?

Just what made the 1936 Husky men's eight crew the stuff of legend? After all, the U.S. had won the men's eight at the previous four Olympics – Navy in 1920, Yale in 1924 (captained by a Rockefeller), and Cal Berkeley in 1928 and 1932.

Many stories characterized the Husky oarsmen as coming from working-class, even hardscrabble roots. This was in large part not true – Bobby Moch's father was a watchmaker and jeweler; Johnny White grew up in the Seward Park neighborhood, his father a steel exporter; Charles Day's dad was a dentist. Only Joe Rantz, who had a lonely childhood and went out on his own at 15, fully fit the legend. All nine, however, spent most of their teen-age years enduring the darkest days of the 【41†Great Depression†historylink.org】, when life was hard for almost everyone.

Then there was where they hailed from – a relatively small university in the Northwest corner of the country. UW's enrollment in 1935 was 9,200; Cal Berkeley's enrollment the same year was 15,500. Navy and Yale had no difficulty funding the equipment and travel of their crews, nor did Cal. Only the Huskies, the best of the lot, had to rely on public generosity to get from event to event.

And there was this – America was coming out of the worst of the Depression in 1936 and was hungry for heroes. The Huskies were thrilling, and like another public hero of the era, the diminutive racehorse Seabiscuit, the crew had the confidence and the skill to hang back until late in a race, then surge ahead with a blazing display of speed, precision, and endurance. In 1936 these nine boys beat the best the West Coast had to offer, the best the rest of the country had to offer, and the best the world had to offer. They fully deserved all the respect and adoration that came their way.

# 1936 US Olympic Rowing Gold Medal Race Footage 

Posted by 【13†Debbie Lang】 | December 19, 2023

As Hitler watched, the US Olympic Rowing Team got off to a horrible start in the men's eight Gold medal race. With the crowd shouting "Deutschland," the US found themselves in the back of the pack by the middle of the 2,000-meter race. Suddenly, Don Hume, who had been battling a respiratory illness, picked up the pace, propelling the team to the front of the pack and a Gold medal win. Corrective Warranty Deeds in Alabama  

You just bought a new house, have your deed in hand, and you are ready to relax in your new home. But after taking another look at the deed, you notice a mistake in the legal description. Now what?  

Alabama law provides for reformation of a deed by judicial intervention under (Ala. Code 1975, 35-4-150), but filing a corrective deed might be an option to resolve simple mistakes.  

A corrective deed is an instrument used to fix an error in a deed that was recorded at an earlier date. It can only be used to correct non-material errors, causing no actual change in the substance of the deed. Common minor errors include misspelled names or missing information, such as marital status, or a mistake transcribing courses and distances in the legal description of the property. Major changes to the substance of the deed, or details that effect how property is titled require a new deed.   

A corrective warranty deed has the same form as the previously recorded warranty deed containing the error and includes all the same information, in addition to correcting the error. The corrective deed states the nature of the error and recites the date and recording information of the erroneous deed.  

The deed must be acknowledged before any of the officers listed in (Ala. Code 1975, 35-4-24). For the corrective deed to be valid, all parties who signed the prior deed must sign the corrective deed in the presence of a notarial official. The execution of a deed must be attested by at least one witness in Alabama (Ala. Code 1975, 35-4-20). If the grantor is married, Alabama requires that both spouses appear before an officer authorized by law to take acknowledgements of deeds and sign the deed (Ala. Code 1975, 6-10-3).   

Most transfers of real property are subject to a privilege or license tax, but corrective deeds are exempt under Ala. Code 1975, 40-22-1, and do not require a Real Estate Sales Validation Form (Form RT-1).  

This article is provided for informational purposes only and is not a substitute for legal advice. Contact a lawyer with questions about corrective warranty deeds or any other issues related to transferring real property in Alabama.

Errors can occur anywhere in the deed: in the legal description of the property or as omission of required information, such as the marital status of the grantor or grantee. The marital status of the grantor is of particular importance since, in the case of sale or mortgage of the homestead, Alabama requires that both spouses appear “before an officer authorized by law to take acknowledgements of deeds” and sign the contract, deed or mortgage (Ala. Code 6-10-3). The spouse may have an inheritance right, sometimes referred to as a dower, curtesy, or statutory share, in the real estate. The spouse usually joins in signing a contract, deed or mortgage as an acknowledgement that the marital portion is part of the conveyance. In terms of the vesting information on the deed, Alabama assumes tenancy in common without rights of survivorship for two or more owners. So the decision to hold title as joint tenants with right of survivorship must be stated explicitly in the deed.

Omissions or errors can also occur in the description of the property itself. Alabama requires a description in metes and bounds. Also, when referring to a plat, attach that plat or describe the plat book or office in which it is located. This applies to all instruments executed after July 21, 1972. If prior deed was recorded before that date and information is unavailable, the grantor or mortgagor must state explicitly “that the plat is lost, destroyed or unavailable for recording” (Ala. Code 35-4-74). 

Submit deeds for recording at the office of the judge of probate in the county where the property is located.

## Frequently Asked Questions:

##### How long does it take to get my forms?

Forms are available immediately after submitting payment.

##### What are supplemental forms?

Often when a deed is recorded, additional documents are required by Alabama or Jefferson County. These could be tax related, informational, or even as simple as a coversheet. Supplemental forms are provided for free with your order where available.

##### How do I get my forms, are they emailed?

Forms are NOT emailed to you. Immediately after you submit payment, the Jefferson County forms you order will be available for download directly from your 【25†account】. You can then download the forms to your computer. If you do not already have an account, one will be created for you as part of the order process, and your login details will be sent to you. If you encounter any issues accessing your forms, please reach out to our support team for assistance.

##### What type of files are the forms?

All of our Jefferson County Correction Warranty Deed forms are PDFs. You will need to have or get Adobe Reader to use our forms. Adobe Reader is free software that most computers already have installed.

##### Can the Correction Warranty Deed forms be re-used?

Yes. You can re-use the forms for your personal use. For example, if you have more than one property in Jefferson County that you need to transfer you would only need to order our forms once for all of your properties in Jefferson County.

##### Are these forms guaranteed to be recordable in Jefferson County?

Yes. Our form blanks are guaranteed to meet or exceed all formatting requirements set forth by Jefferson County including margin requirements, content requirements, font and font size requirements.

##### Do I have to enter all of my property information online?

No. The blank forms are downloaded to your computer and you fill them out there, at your convenience.

##### Can I save the completed form, email it to someone?

Yes, you can save your deed form at any point with your information in it. The forms can also be emailed, blank or complete, as attachments.

##### Do I need any special software to use these forms?

You will need to have Adobe Reader installed on your computer to use our forms. Adobe Reader is free software that most computers already have installed.

##### Are there any recurring fees involved?

No. Nothing to cancel, no memberships, no recurring fees.

Errors can occur anywhere in the deed: in the legal description of the property or as omission of required information, such as the marital status of the grantor or grantee. The marital status of the grantor is of particular importance since, in the case of sale or mortgage of the homestead, Alabama requires that both spouses appear “before an officer authorized by law to take acknowledgements of deeds” and sign the contract, deed or mortgage (Ala. Code 6-10-3). The spouse may have an inheritance right, sometimes referred to as a dower, curtesy, or statutory share, in the real estate. The spouse usually joins in signing a contract, deed or mortgage as an acknowledgement that the marital portion is part of the conveyance. In terms of the vesting information on the deed, Alabama assumes tenancy in common without rights of survivorship for two or more owners. So the decision to hold title as joint tenants with right of survivorship must be stated explicitly in the deed.

Omissions or errors can also occur in the description of the property itself. Alabama requires a description in metes and bounds. Also, when referring to a plat, attach that plat or describe the plat book or office in which it is located. This applies to all instruments executed after July 21, 1972. If prior deed was recorded before that date and information is unavailable, the grantor or mortgagor must state explicitly “that the plat is lost, destroyed or unavailable for recording” (Ala. Code 35-4-74). 

Submit deeds for recording at the office of the judge of probate in the county where the property is located.

- Obtain the Corrective Warranty Deed Form: Download the form online, usually available in PDF format.

- Tax Exemption: Corrective deeds are generally exempt from privilege or license tax in Alabama.

## Frequently Asked Questions:

##### How long does it take to get my forms?

Forms are available immediately after submitting payment.

##### What are supplemental forms?

Often when a deed is recorded, additional documents are required by Alabama or Jefferson County. These could be tax related, informational, or even as simple as a coversheet. Supplemental forms are provided for free with your order where available.

##### How do I get my forms, are they emailed?

Forms are NOT emailed to you. Immediately after you submit payment, the Jefferson County forms you order will be available for download directly from your 【25†account】. You can then download the forms to your computer. If you do not already have an account, one will be created for you as part of the order process, and your login details will be sent to you. If you encounter any issues accessing your forms, please reach out to our support team for assistance.

##### What type of files are the forms?

All of our Jefferson County Correction Warranty Deed forms are PDFs. You will need to have or get Adobe Reader to use our forms. Adobe Reader is free software that most computers already have installed.

Yes. You can re-use the forms for your personal use. For example, if you have more than one property in Jefferson County that you need to transfer you would only need to order our forms once for all of your properties in Jefferson County.

##### Do I have to enter all of my property information online?

No. The blank forms are downloaded to your computer and you fill them out there, at your convenience.

##### Can I save the completed form, email it to someone?

Yes, you can save your deed form at any point with your information in it. The forms can also be emailed, blank or complete, as attachments.

##### Do I need any special software to use these forms?

You will need to have Adobe Reader installed on your computer to use our forms. Adobe Reader is free software that most computers already have installed.

No. Nothing to cancel, no memberships, no recurring fees.

## What is the Alabama Correction Warranty Deed

Corrective Warranty Deeds in Alabama  

You just bought a new house, have your deed in hand, and you are ready to relax in your new home. But after taking another look at the deed, you notice a mistake in the legal description. Now what?  

Alabama law provides for reformation of a deed by judicial intervention under (Ala. Code 1975, 35-4-150), but filing a corrective deed might be an option to resolve simple mistakes.  

A corrective deed is an instrument used to fix an error in a deed that was recorded at an earlier date. It can only be used to correct non-material errors, causing no actual change in the substance of the deed. Common minor errors include misspelled names or missing information, such as marital status, or a mistake transcribing courses and distances in the legal description of the property. Major changes to the substance of the deed, or details that effect how property is titled require a new deed.   

A corrective warranty deed has the same form as the previously recorded warranty deed containing the error and includes all the same information, in addition to correcting the error. The corrective deed states the nature of the error and recites the date and recording information of the erroneous deed.  

The deed must be acknowledged before any of the officers listed in (Ala. Code 1975, 35-4-24). For the corrective deed to be valid, all parties who signed the prior deed must sign the corrective deed in the presence of a notarial official. The execution of a deed must be attested by at least one witness in Alabama (Ala. Code 1975, 35-4-20). If the grantor is married, Alabama requires that both spouses appear before an officer authorized by law to take acknowledgements of deeds and sign the deed (Ala. Code 1975, 6-10-3).   

Most transfers of real property are subject to a privilege or license tax, but corrective deeds are exempt under Ala. Code 1975, 40-22-1, and do not require a Real Estate Sales Validation Form (Form RT-1).

Errors can occur anywhere in the deed: in the legal description of the property or as omission of required information, such as the marital status of the grantor or grantee. The marital status of the grantor is of particular importance since, in the case of sale or mortgage of the homestead, Alabama requires that both spouses appear “before an officer authorized by law to take acknowledgements of deeds” and sign the contract, deed or mortgage (Ala. Code 6-10-3). The spouse may have an inheritance right, sometimes referred to as a dower, curtesy, or statutory share, in the real estate. The spouse usually joins in signing a contract, deed or mortgage as an acknowledgement that the marital portion is part of the conveyance. In terms of the vesting information on the deed, Alabama assumes tenancy in common without rights of survivorship for two or more owners. So the decision to hold title as joint tenants with right of survivorship must be stated explicitly in the deed.

Omissions or errors can also occur in the description of the property itself. Alabama requires a description in metes and bounds. Also, when referring to a plat, attach that plat or describe the plat book or office in which it is located. This applies to all instruments executed after July 21, 1972. If prior deed was recorded before that date and information is unavailable, the grantor or mortgagor must state explicitly “that the plat is lost, destroyed or unavailable for recording” (Ala. Code 35-4-74). 

Submit deeds for recording at the office of the judge of probate in the county where the property is located.

## What is the Alabama Correction Warranty Deed

Corrective Warranty Deeds in Alabama  

You just bought a new house, have your deed in hand, and you are ready to relax in your new home. But after taking another look at the deed, you notice a mistake in the legal description. Now what?  

Alabama law provides for reformation of a deed by judicial intervention under (Ala. Code 1975, 35-4-150), but filing a corrective deed might be an option to resolve simple mistakes.  

A corrective deed is an instrument used to fix an error in a deed that was recorded at an earlier date. It can only be used to correct non-material errors, causing no actual change in the substance of the deed. Common minor errors include misspelled names or missing information, such as marital status, or a mistake transcribing courses and distances in the legal description of the property. Major changes to the substance of the deed, or details that effect how property is titled require a new deed.   

A corrective warranty deed has the same form as the previously recorded warranty deed containing the error and includes all the same information, in addition to correcting the error. The corrective deed states the nature of the error and recites the date and recording information of the erroneous deed.  

The deed must be acknowledged before any of the officers listed in (Ala. Code 1975, 35-4-24). For the corrective deed to be valid, all parties who signed the prior deed must sign the corrective deed in the presence of a notarial official. The execution of a deed must be attested by at least one witness in Alabama (Ala. Code 1975, 35-4-20). If the grantor is married, Alabama requires that both spouses appear before an officer authorized by law to take acknowledgements of deeds and sign the deed (Ala. Code 1975, 6-10-3).   

Most transfers of real property are subject to a privilege or license tax, but corrective deeds are exempt under Ala. Code 1975, 40-22-1, and do not require a Real Estate Sales Validation Form (Form RT-1).  

This article is provided for informational purposes only and is not a substitute for legal advice. Contact a lawyer with questions about corrective warranty deeds or any other issues related to transferring real property in Alabama.

# Creating Value and Sustaining Our Forests

For every tree that Green Diamond’s forests grow, an abundant stream of value follows.

From carbon solutions to renewable sources of energy, working forests produce far more than meets the eye. We continue to grow our business by innovating new ways to make the most of the forest’s natural resources—always with the prosperity and health of future generations and forests in mind.

[Image 7] 

## Timber

Our primary source of revenue is 【36†sustainably harvested timber.】 Third-party certified to one of the world’s two leading sustainable forest management standards, customers rely on us for a quality product they can trust.

[Image 8] 

## Chips

In a properly managed forest, almost nothing goes to waste. Our 【37†wood chip business】 utilizes residual wood from timber and lumber production, which is used to create paper products, renewable energy and more. 

[Image 9] 

## Co-Investment and Forest Management

Leveraging more than a century of expertise, we provide 【38†active forest management】, responsible harvesting and log marketing services as a co-investor in various forestry operations.

Properly managed forests are unmatched in their ability to absorb and store carbon. We are among the largest owner-operators of 【39†natural climate solutions】, which aim to materially increase carbon sequestration and produce third-party-validated carbon offsets. 

[Image 11] 

## Renewable Energy and Biomass

Our forests produce wood fiber—or 【40†biomass】—products that customers can convert into a renewable source of energy to generate electricity for power plants, heat homes and even produce jet fuel.
